articles.title: Firms scramble for battery power in Spain and Portugal
articles.summary: After last year's massive power failure Spanish and Portuguese firms are buying battery back ups.
articles.body:
On the 28 April last year, Portugal and Spain went dark for several hours.

A massive power failure caused widespread chaos . People dug out lanterns and old radios, and companies scrambled to save what production they could.

The Spanish meat processing firm Fribin, in Binéfar, in the north eastern province of Aragon, was midway through its morning shift when the sudden shutdown brought production lines to a halt.

For Andrés Altabás, Fribin's technology and systems director, it was a nightmarish situation.

Emergency systems didn't have the capacity for continued operation. "Refrigeration was prioritised but all the lines had to be stopped," he adds.

Many tonnes of meat in the processing stage had to be discarded. "There were losses of hundreds of thousands of euros," says Altabás.

The bosses at Fribin realised they had to rethink their back up plans.

It was a big undertaking as the company's energy needs are "quite large", amounting to more than 25 gigawatt-hours a year, most of it for refrigeration.

The business had been considering investing in a battery back-up system for years, but it had been judged too expensive.

"And then came the blackout, and all of that together catalysed the investment," Altabás tells the BBC.

The first purchase of a five megawatt-hour module was made in June 2025, and a second module with the same storage capacity was ordered in early June 2026, both amounting to a total investment of around €1.5m (£1.3m; $1.7m), funded in part by the European Union's Next Generation funds.

Firms across Europe have been switching to electricity from fossil fuels for their industrial needs, encouraged by subsidies from EU funds.

While that is helping bring down emissions of climate-warming gases, it has also made firms more vulnerable to power cuts.

And in Spain and Portugal that threat was made painfully clear last year.

On both sides of the border, firms are looking for ways to avoid disruption.

"The industrial sector has been one of the first to look at storage systems, since it can't have its production drop off too abruptly," says Miguel Matias, founder of the Portuguese energy services company Self Energy, headquartered in the UK.

"A backup for a few hours, or even minutes, might guarantee that machines don't get damaged," he says.

And there have been more recent incidents to spur investment.

At the end of January, Storm Kristin toppled thousands of electricity and telecom poles across central Portugal, cutting power and communications to hundreds of thousands of people - some for weeks.

So, companies and other organisations have been taking action.

In Spain, battery storage capacity has risen almost sevenfold since last April, from about 28 MW before the blackout to 193MW in April 2026, according to the grid operator Red Eléctrica.

In December, the IDAE, Spain's Institute for the Diversification and Saving of Energy, awarded €827m in EU funds to 133 energy storage projects totalling 2,400MW. Around 80% of that is battery storage.

The new capacity will be close to 10 times the amount that Red Eléctrica currently registers on the Spanish grid.

It's all good news for battery suppliers.

"We are seeing not only an increase in demand, but also a clear evolution in customer requirements," says Alberto Bodegas, from battery storage company Sungrow.

Traditionally, commercial and industrial clients were looking for partial or full backup solutions, Bodegas says.

Today, Bodegas says customers are demanding more advanced capabilities, such as seamless backup, meaning the switch from grid to backup occurs instantaneously and without any noticeable interruption.

This is particularly critical for sensitive environments such as hospitals and data centres.

Delivery times are also crucial for buyers, currently under tight deadlines linked to EU funding programmes. Battery companies are being pressed to meet increasingly shorter delivery dates, Bodegas says.

Portugal's Vista Alegre, the oldest and largest porcelain maker in the Iberian country, decided to install energy storage systems in 2022, seizing the opportunity of abundant funds from the EU's Recovery and Resilience Plan.

"The blackout ultimately served, above all, to accelerate this process," Emília Encarnação of Vista Alegre explains. The company's facilities in the coastal city of Ílhavo, in the province of Aveiro, are now equipped with modules with around 2MWh of storage capacity.

"The blackout caused some irreparable losses, particularly at the plants operating on a continuous production basis, where sudden power interruptions have a direct impact on production processes," Encarnação recalls.

Advantages go beyond being able to respond to sudden shocks in the energy network. For example installing batteries also means the company can profit from selling energy into the general network.

At Primus Ceramics, located near the city of Aveiro, in central Portugal, a diesel generator saved the day during last year's blackout.

Their roller kilns - which transport materials through every production phase inside industrial ovens - are powered by electric motors.

During the power cut, the generator kept the products rolling, minimising the day's losses.

The experience accelerated the company's plan to make their production process more resilient, company CEO Paulo Almeida tells the BBC.

Primus already had two batteries installed in 2022 to back-up their energy supply and for selling electricity back to their energy company when market conditions were favourable.

By the end of this year Primus will have more than double its battery capacity, to store more energy from the factory's solar panels.

For Almeida, that would be reassuring after the stress of last year's blackout.

"We were at it until eight, nine at night, deciding whether we should stop, whether we should lower the furnace temperatures, or whether we'd take the risk and wait for the power to come back in time," he says.

The power did come back in time, but it was near miss for Primus.

articles.title: Warriors signing Georges Niang, Brandon Williams: How they fit with Golden State
articles.summary: The Warriors are signing Brandon Williams and Georges Niang to one-year deals. Here's how the players fit with Golden State.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors have had a rather quiet offseason that returned many familiar faces from last season's roster. Now, they have added two newcomers at the guard and forward positions.

The Warriors agreed to sign 6-foot-1 point guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million deal, according to ESPN NBA insider Shams Charania . Golden State also agreed to sign free agent forward Georges Niang to a one-year, $3.9 million deal, Charania reported.

Williams spent the 2025-26 season with the Dallas Mavericks , where he averaged career highs with 13 points and 3.9 assists in 66 games. Williams averaged 22.2 minutes per night, the most playing time he's seen since joining the NBA as an undrafted rookie signing in 2021.

Williams was on the Mavericks' roster the previous three seasons. He first entered the league playing for the Portland Trail Blazers , where he averaged 12.9 points in 24 games in 2021-22.

The veteran Niang has averaged 7.4 points per game across 544 NBA games, but did not play in 2025-26 due to injury.

The fifth-year NBA player joins a guard-heavy team already featuring the likes of Stephen Curry , Brandin Podziemski , Moses Moody , Will Richard , LJ Cryer , Gary Payton II and De'Anthony Melton.

Williams will seemingly be a spark off the bench for Golden State. It's a role Williams is familiar with and the Warriors know how dynamic he can be torching other second units − they got a taste of that work last season.

Williams had one of his best games against the Warriors on Christmas Day 2025, while with the Mavericks. Williams seemingly couldn't miss that day. He tallied 26 points on 9-for-12 shooting from the field.

He scored a career-high against the Memphis Grizzlies on March 7, 2025 when he went off for 31 points on 10-for-15 shooting, including 4-of-8 on 3-point field goals. He added six assists, five rebounds and a steal to his stat line. Williams showcased his ability to get to the rim and draw contact that game, getting to the free throw line eight times, making seven.

If healthy, Niang brings another 3-point shooting threat to the Warriors roster. He fits in all too well.

After a decade in the NBA, Niang has proved to be a reliable role player and credible 3-point shooter who connects from deep at a 40% clip for his career.

Niang missed the 2025-26 season due to a foot injury. The Warriors were all too familiar with injuries last season, with Curry, Moody, Jimmy Butler III and Al Horford among the big names impacted.

Niang has played for the Indiana Pacers , Utah Jazz , Philadelphia 76ers , Cleveland Cavaliers and Atlanta Hawks . He was going to return to the Jazz after a trade last offseason because the team felt his veteran presence would benefit their young core. Niang joining the Warriors' mix of veteran leadership and young reserves should be the perfect storm.

Plus, Niang should be somewhat familiar with the Warriors' organization and development system having played for their G-League affiliate, the Santa Cruz Warriors, during the 2017-18 season.

Williams won't have too much of a time getting acclimated with the Warriors and how they operate. He is already familiar with a member of the team.

Williams is a 26-year-old guard from Los Angeles . He attended Crespi Carmelite High School in Encino, California, where he was teammates with Melton. They dominated the floor when they shared the space. Melton averaged 20 points and Williams averaged 15.8 points as they led the Celts to a 33-5 record and won the CIF Division I state championship.

The two celebrated Williams' signing, posting a screen grab from their FaceTime video call showing both smiling as Williams quoted the tagline for hip-hop producer Chandler "Turbo" Durham.

"RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton," Williams posted on X, formerly Twitter, with blue and yellow hearts symbolizing the Warriors' color-scheme.

RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton 💛💙 pic.twitter.com/tyoarMA0R7 — Brandon Williams (@TheeBWill) August 25, 2026

RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton 💛💙 pic.twitter.com/tyoarMA0R7

Although not Southern California, Williams is back on the West Coast, so that has to be a breath of fresh air for him. His familiarity with Melton should help make for a smooth transition to the Bay Area.

articles.title: Iconic Bitcoin mine pivots to AI as industry turns back on crypto
articles.summary: The price of Bitcoin has risen in August but is still far below its peak almost a year ago - and companies are refitting their mines.
articles.body:
Companies that once filled warehouses with computers to earn Bitcoin - a process known as mining - are now using that computing power for AI.

Bitcoin mining companies invested large sums on giant banks of powerful computers as the price of Bitcoin rocketed in recent years .

But those mining companies have faced falling rewards since the value of the cryptocurrency has slumped from its peak in October 2025.

Now many are pivoting to AI and signing deals with companies such as Anthropic - who are spending billions of dollars on the infrastructure needed to keep up in the AI race.

Bitcoin mining and other key cryptocurrency terms explained Published 5 June

Bitcoin mining and other key cryptocurrency terms explained

Like AI systems, Bitcoin relies on vast networks of powerful computers housed in data centres.

Because Bitcoin operates without a central authority, these computers verify transactions and are rewarded with newly-created digital coins.

But the rewards have reduced and the value of coins has dropped since last year.

One bitcoin was worth about $124,000 (Â£91,000) at its peak in October 2025, but has since fallen sharply.

More recently, it has rallied to around $80,000 - meaning it is up almost 30% so far in August.

But, for companies that have already made the change, even that may not be enough to get them to return to the crypto industry, because the switch of use - once made - is expensive to undo.

Industry analysts say Bitcoin mining companies have been pivoting to AI because they have years of experience in finding cheap electricity and efficiently running large data centres.

TerraWulf, Ionic Digital, Core Scientific, Iris Energy, Bitdeer, Riot Platforms and Hut 8 are just some of the companies increasingly diverting investment and infrastructure from bitcoin mining towards AI.

Riot Platforms signed a $9bn, 20-year compute deal with Anthropic earlier this month.

Company names and websites are changing to reflect the shift too.

Applied Blockchain has become Applied Digital.

TerraWulf's website once described the firm as an "infrastructure-focused bitcoin mining company".

It now says it focuses on "next-generation AI and high-performance computing".

Enegix, which opened a huge Bitcoin mining site in Kazakhstan to great fanfare in 2020, is now pivoting too.

"Today, we are moving confidently towards artificial intelligence and planning the gradual alignment of our energy and infrastructure capabilities, both in Kazakhstan and elsewhere, towards the development of AI infrastructure," said the company's chief executive Yerbolsyn Sarsenov.

Enegix says it is in active discussions with AI and HPC (high-performance computing) companies and planning to transform a "significant" portion of the business to AI.

But refitting crypto mines for AI is expensive and in some cases the companies have had to sell some of their Bitcoin holdings to fund the switch.

Wolfie Zhao from The Energy Mag - a publication that rebranded from The Miner Mag to reflect the trend - predicts the industry pivot will continue even as the price of Bitcoin has risen in recent days.

"We expect to see many public miners continue winding down their Bitcoin mining hardware in the coming quarters," he said.

Asked if the shift away from Bitcoin mining might affect the security or stability of the cryptocurrency, Zhao said he hoped more miners will enter the market as conditions improve.

But he predicted many of the big players would not easily be able to switch back to Bitcoin.

"Once that multi-gigawatt power infrastructure has been retrofitted to AI or HPC colocation, there is no turning back," he said.

"You can unplug from the Bitcoin network any time but signing a GPU colocation lease for 10 or 20 years means steady revenue and a commitment to keep the infrastructure up for the tenants."

Bitdeer, which claims to be the largest Bitcoin miner in the world, just announced a 16-year deal to provide compute for Anthropic.

But the company's chief strategy officer, Haris Basit, said Bitdeer will continue mining Bitcoin, believing many operators would ultimately pursue a dual-purpose model.

"Bitcoin mining is particularly well suited to that model because it is flexible and interruptible, while AI workloads can provide longer-duration contracted revenues," he said.

articles.title: UK weather: Met Office warnings in force amid thunderstorm and flood risk
articles.summary: Torrential downpours will affect parts of England and Wales, delivering some of the wettest weather in several weeks
articles.body:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

The Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning covers a large swathe of England and Wales.

A band of showers and thunderstorms will push northwards during Wednesday morning with sunny spells following from the south.

However, further scattered downpours and storms will spring up during the afternoon.

As many as 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) of rain could fall in some locations within just an hour, and it is even possible that 40-50mm (1.6-2in) could accumulate over a few hours.

However, due to the hit-and-miss nature of showers, some places will miss the rain and weather apps may struggle to get the detail of the forecast correct.

Where the rain does fall, flash flooding is a real concern. This will be especially problematic where the ground is hard after the prolonged dry spell, making it difficult for the water to soak in.

Difficult driving conditions are expected with the chance that some roads could be closed.

Large hail and frequent lightning are also possible.

Northern Ireland will also see some showers but these are likely to be less intense with less thunder.

Many parts of Scotland will remain dry with sunny spells, although some showers are likely in the south-west later.

Thursday will bring another zone of thunderstorms, again affecting mostly England and Wales.

The Met Office has issued a further yellow weather warning, valid from 06:00 until 22:00 BST.

Widespread rainfall totals of 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) are expected in the warning area within three hours, while some areas could see 50mm (2in) within the same timeframe.

There is a small chance that eastern-facing hills - exposed to easterly winds - could record 75mm (3in) during 12 hours, which would bring a significant flood risk.

The showers may eventually reach southern Scotland and Northern Ireland but are likely to weaken and become less intense as they drift northwards.

Wettest weather in weeks for parts of southern UK

Despite a period of unsettled weather last week, some southern parts of the UK have still seen barely any rain recently.

Brize Norton in Oxfordshire has recorded just 0.4mm of rain so far this August, less than 1% of what it would normally expect during the month as a whole.

Kew Gardens recorded no rain at all in July, and only 1.8mm so far this month.

It means the rain we are expecting this week is likely to far outstrip what has fallen recently in some areas.

What does 80 per cent chance of rain mean? Published 12 June

What does 80 per cent chance of rain mean?

Why you may not see showers and thunderstorms on your weather app

Thunderstorms are often very hit-and-miss.

Some places can see flooding downpours while others, perhaps only a few miles away, avoid the heaviest rain and stay essentially dry.

Weather apps - including the BBC Weather app - can struggle in these scenarios.

Forecasters know that the conditions are ripe for storms to form, with warm humid air across the UK interacting with a zone of colder air pushing in from the west, higher in the atmosphere.

This generates low pressure and instability.

However, the computer weather models that drive weather apps will always struggle to pinpoint exactly where and when the biggest storms will spring up.

It is a bit like heating popcorn kernels in a pan.

You cannot know precisely which kernels will pop and in which order, while some kernels may not pop at all.

Some of the storms will also occur at night, which may mean they do not show up in the daily weather icons.

It is worth keeping an eye on the hourly weather symbols, as well as the percentage chances of rain, if you are making outdoor plans.

articles.title: Deloitte to pay $21.5 million to settle US government probe over DEI
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Accounting firm Deloitte will pay $21. Department of Justice probe over diversity, equity and inclusion ‌practices, which Pres...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Accounting firm Deloitte will pay $21.5 million to settle a U.S. Department of Justice probe over diversity, equity and inclusion ‌practices, which President Donald Trump's administration has cracked down on during his ‌second term in office.

The settlement marks a resolution reached through the DOJ's unit formed last year called the "Civil ​Rights Fraud Initiative" to crack down on DEI policies using a civil anti-fraud law.

The Trump administration has targeted public and private organizations, from government agencies to universities, over DEI practices that civil rights advocates say help address historic inequities for marginalized groups like women, the LGBT ‌community and ethnic minorities.

The White ⁠House casts DEI as anti-merit and discriminatory against groups such as white people and men. Trump has signed executive orders asking federal contractors ⁠and subcontractors to eliminate DEI. Civil rights groups say such steps are rolling back social progress.

Many U.S. companies scaled back or modified diversity policies after Trump's orders.

The DOJ said on Tuesday ​that ​business units within Deloitte received monthly summaries tracking ​the "demographic goals" and alleged that Deloitte's ‌Partners, Principals and Managing Directors were evaluated, in part, based on their contributions to helping Deloitte achieve its workforce composition goals.

The DOJ alleged that such DEI goals aimed at improving the representation of the Black and Hispanic communities impacted promotion decisions.

Deloitte denies it engaged in discriminatory conduct and the settlement agreement released on Tuesday said it does not amount ‌to an admission of liability. The company said ​it was pleased to resolve the matter to "avoid the ​cost and distraction of protracted ​litigation."

The Justice Department's settlement also resolves claims filed by the American Alliance ‌for Equal Rights, a group founded by ​affirmative action opponent ​Edward Blum, pursuant to the U.S. False Claims Act, which allows whistleblowers to sue companies on the government's behalf to recover taxpayer funds paid out based on ​false claims.

Whistleblowers are entitled to ‌a cut of any recovery in such cases. Under the settlement agreement, ​Blum's group will receive $4.3 million, the DOJ said.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh, Ismail Shakil ​and Nate Raymond; Editing by Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Ball python 'Tippy' found caged in community garden as animal control seeks owner
articles.summary: Residents and garden staff told 311 they had seen someone leave the snake in a cage beside the garden beds.
articles.body:
A routine stream of found-pet notices in Boston took an unexpected turn when city officials shared an alert for a ball python, rather than the more familiar missing dog or cat.

A caged snake later identified as "Tippy" was discovered near the raised beds of a Dorchester community food garden, Boston.com reported .

Boston Animal Care and Control said the ball python turned up at about 6 p.m. at a community garden on Ellington Street in Dorchester, per the outlet. The animal arrived there under mysterious circumstances.

Before animal control arrived, residents and garden staff told 311 they had seen someone leave the snake in a cage beside the garden beds, a spokesperson told Boston.com.

An officer brought the reptile to the city's animal care facility in Roslindale, where officials said it was in good condition and getting proper care.

articles.title: The backlash Pride faces from inside and outside the LGBT community
articles.summary: Big companies used to go out of their way to support Pride. Now, there's a nervousness in the air, Darren Milby writes
articles.body:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

Pride started as a protest, with Britain's first official Pride march in London in 1972. Homosexuality was illegal in the UK until 1967, and LGBT people lost jobs and housing because of their sexuality, while police forces frequently targeted the community with raids and surveillance that made everyday life precarious.

In Manchester, Pride started small in 1985. A bringâandâbuy sale on Canal Street was organised to raise money to spruce up the rather drab-looking hospital ward treating those with HIV and Aids at the height of the epidemic.

Little did those early attendees realise how big Manchester Pride would become: a four-day, city centre extravaganza over the August bank holiday weekend, with colourful floats, loud music, and every inch of pavement filled with enthusiastic spectators dressed to the nines, streaked with rainbow face paint.

By 2019, the event had outgrown the city's famous Gay Village. That year's headline act, American superstar Ariana Grande, performed in a purpose-built stage in another part of Manchester - for a premium ticket price. It prompted criticism, and the organisers of Manchester Pride would later come under fire for ending funding for various charities (including an HIV charity, and a scheme that distributed free condoms).

The company behind Manchester Pride went into voluntary liquidation last year, owing more than Â£1m to suppliers and performers, including Nelly Furtado. Since its collapse, local businesses and charities have created a not-for-profit group - Manchester Village Pride - with the aim of organising a much cheaper festival more rooted in the community.

Carl Austin-Behan, who is helping to organise this year's scaled-back event, says he's been "frustrated for a number of years" by the direction of Manchester Pride. "When things were being taken out of the village, that was the first sign that things were going in the wrong directionâ¦ It should be about the community. We certainly don't need to be spending the amount of money that was spent on Manchester Pride."

And Manchester's problems aren't isolated. London Pride has faced criticism for feeling overly corporate and overcrowded; Brighton has struggled with the financial burden of staging largeâscale concerts and policing. Against that backdrop, smaller events like Crewe seem to be the direction many Prides are going in 2026.

But the political winds have also changed - with seemingly less corporate enthusiasm for diversity and inclusion initiatives.

Phil Douglas, organiser of Newcastle Pride, says: "There is a general nervousness from organisations and companies to be front and centre in their support. We see some wanting to still support us but not wanting their logo attachedâ¦ they don't want the backlash which is right there ready in the online community. It's quite a complex time to navigate support for Prides as a whole."

A few years ago, you couldn't go on social media in June - known as "Pride month" - without seeing what felt like every corporate logo incorporating the Pride flag. Critics called it "rainbowâwashing", arguing that the displays of solidarity were more about marketing than meaningful action.

But now, according to Guardian analysis, the corporate presence has been waning. Last year, mentions of Pride on social media by the UK's 10 biggest listed or headquartered companies had fallen by 92% compared with 2023 - a drop that suggests brands are pulling back from overt LGBT messaging.

"There has been a general rowing back of corporate support for LGBT causes globally," says Paul Martin, chief executive of the LGBT Foundation charity. "We've seen that with politics changing in some countries and diversity and inclusion being seen as too wokeâ¦ We don't get support from some quarters like we used to.

"And that has played out with Pride festivals as well. Corporate funding has been pulled back and that has caused a real challenge for Pride organisers to balance the books."

A survey by the pollster Ipsos found that the share of British adults who want companies and brands to promote LGBT rights dipped from 52% in 2021 to 44% this year.

In Liverpool, Merseyside Police did not take part in the city's Pride parade last year after legal advice warned that uniformed participation by a public body could breach rules on political impartiality.

This summer, firefighters and police again stayed away: Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said it was taking a "pragmatic approach" following a High Court ruling that found officers in the northâeast should not have been allowed to join a Pride event. West Midlands Ambulance Service also withdrew from Birmingham Pride on similar legal advice.

Back in May's local elections in England, Reform UK won power on 14 councils, adding to the 10 they already controlled. Last month, the party's leader, Nigel Farage, said he is "fine" with Pride events going ahead but did not want local authorities to promote them.

A few weeks after taking power in Durham last year, the town's new Reform administration removed a rainbow flag from the council headquarters. Councillors also withdrew their funding contribution of Â£2,500 for Durham Pride. In the Merseyside town of St Helens, meanwhile, the Reform council leader instructed officials to cease engagement with all aspects of Pride; the council also removed displays celebrating the festival from libraries.

Explaining the cuts to funding, Reform's Darren Grimes, deputy leader of Durham Council, says: "I feel that we've moved away from that laudable aim of gay equality. We achieved same-sex marriage and that was the final frontier."

Durham Pride organiser Mel Metcalf says taking the flag down made LGBT people in the community "feel unwelcome". The festival did still take place; organisers said it was their "biggest" year ever, after raising around Â£25,000 from individual donors and trade unions.

As well as Reform's approach, the new Conservative council leader in Enfield, north London, has said they will only fly certain flags outside Enfield Civic Centre - and the rainbow flag is not one of them.

Debate around trans rights is also fuelling the Pride culture war. Some gay and lesbian people who describe themselves as "gender critical" - and whose beliefs mean they're sceptical of some of the aims of the trans rights movement - say they feel sidelined by Pride; while some trans people say they no longer feel safe attending.

A lesbian woman who describes herself as gender critical, and did not want to be named, told me she no longer attends Pride because she thinks it has become dominated by a focus on trans issues.

Grimes, one of Reform's highest-profile gay members, argues that Pride has moved away from its focus on gay equality and become bound up with the wider gender identity debate: "You've slain the dragon in the pursuit of equality and now all you are left with is a few rambling sheep." He says that "public subsidy" for LGBT issues has become a "cash cow" that fuels "narratives of victimhood".

For some, the focus on trans rights is a reason to step back from Pride; for others, it underscores why events like Sparkle matter.

Sparkle is the UK's biggest transgender celebration. It takes place in late June in Manchester's Gay Village, a few months before the Pride weekend. This year's event had live music and comedy. Lauren, a transgender volunteer at the event, told me: "We've got a lot of stigma and hatred against usâ¦ You've got people trying to push us back into the dark and it does make it harder to live our lives."

Another transgender woman I spoke to, who was staying in a hotel in Manchester's Gay Village, said she wanted to be in the city for the event, but was wary of leaving the hotel because she felt unsafe.

Security has also become a central consideration, especially after the events of last month in Berlin, when 21-year-old Abdul Ballout drove a car into a crowd at the city's Pride festival, killing one woman and injuring 29 others. Guy Mathias, from the Security Commonwealth - a trade group for security firms - says he thinks many Pride organisers will review their plans following the Berlin attack.

"Smaller events generally would cost less individually, but they still need many of the same safety measures in place," he adds.

Others think that Pride festivals can create headaches for local residents. Andy Winter, a columnist for the Brighton Argus, attended Pride marches in the 1980s in his role as a Brighton councillor. He recalled in one piece how he was vilified by the press at the time for supporting a pro-LGBT council motion. But last year, he wrote that Brighton's Pride weekend comes with "alcohol and drug-fuelled excesses".

He wrote: "Even though I am not gay, Pride impacts on me. One of the parks I use is 'closed' for ten days... to allow largely straight performers to entertain those able to pay the large entry fee." He added: "The streets are littered with plastics and broken glass. I pity neighbours of the park and surrounding streets who see their driveways and gardens used as toilets."

I've been to dozens of Pride events over the years. Manchester has always been a must. When I was a teenager in Ulverston, Cumbria - a place where I was pretty certain I was the only gay in the village - Manchester always seemed like the bright lights, a land where you could be free and your true self.

This year I'll return again, excited to catch up with my friends and intrigued to see what the new community-focused Pride is all about.

But I suspect there'll be a slightly different mood in the air this year; an awareness that in some parts of the country, Pride has become controversial.

Younger LGBT people still say Pride matters. A 2024 YouGov survey of more than 500 LGBT Britons, aged 16 to 24, found that 90% say it is "very" or "fairly" important that Pride month still exists.

As a young man, I eventually left Ulverston to live in Manchester. But this summer I took a trip back to my old hometown for their Pride festival, a tradition still in its infancy.

The once-familiar cobbled streets looked so different to how I remembered them, lined with cheering locals clapping and filming on phones as a procession bedecked in rainbow flags swept past, led by a brass band playing upbeat gay anthems. It felt a world away from Manchester's famous pop stars and stages covered in corporate logos.

Matt had a similar reflection on returning to Crewe. "What really resonated with me and blew my mind was the fact that it was so family-centred. These small towns put on events that are for the community first and foremost."

As I looked around Ulverston, the national debates that have shaped Pride in recent years felt distant. I was distracted by the small things: people laughing, the spread of ages in attendance. It was the community my teenage self never would have imagined he'd see.

articles.title: Game Thread: Rangers (66-66) at White Sox (68-63)
articles.summary: Anthony Kay and the South Siders look to rebound from Monday’s rough loss
articles.body:
A blowout loss is a tough way to start a series at home in a playoff race, but the South Siders hope to flush Monday's game and come out strong behind Anthony Kay today. After defeating the Sox yesterday, the Rangers now hold a half-game lead over the Houston Astros in the AL West, while Chicago 's lead in the AL Central has shrunk to just 2 1/2 games over the Cleveland Guardians . The Guardians have rebounded from their rough stretch, winning seven of their last 10 and riding a five-game winning streak after defeating the Los Angeles Angels yesterday. The Angels, of course, had opportunities to come back but naturally didn't.

The South Siders are 5-5 in their last 10, and the offense has been struggling as a whole lately, basically living and dying by the long ball as we've seen in the last several games. In August, the White Sox are hitting just .208 with runners in scoring position as a team — the second-worst average in baseball over that stretch — while also racking up the most strikeouts (70). It also probably doesn't help that both Colson Montgomery and Munetaka Murakami are building Strikeout City from the ground up, with Colson leading MLB in Ks over the last two weeks (24 in 51 ABs) and Mune's 21 ranking third in baseball. Woof.

With both the rotation and bullpen continuing to struggle, the pitching staff took another hit when the White Sox announced that Huascar Brazobán is headed to the IL with a left lat strain. Righthander Jonathan Cannon is being called up from Triple-A Charlotte to help fill the hole. Jonathan Cannon is most certainly not the answer, but at this point, the front office seems ready to try anything.

Prior to tonight’s game vs. Texas, the Chicago White Sox placed right-handed pitcher Huáscar Brazobán on the 15-day injured list with a left lat strain and recalled right-handed pitcher Jonathan Cannon from Class AAA Charlotte. — Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) August 25, 2026

Prior to tonight’s game vs. Texas, the Chicago White Sox placed right-handed pitcher Huáscar Brazobán on the 15-day injured list with a left lat strain and recalled right-handed pitcher Jonathan Cannon from Class AAA Charlotte.

The only other roster update for today is that our sweet (mostly) clutch Andrew Benintendi has been placed on the bereavement list, and Rikuu Nishida will rejoin the team in his absence. We send our thoughts to Andrew and his family during this time.

Prior to tonight’s game vs. Texas, the Chicago White Sox placed outfielder Andrew Benintendi on the Bereavement/Family Medical Emergency List and recalled infielder/outfielder Rikuu Nishida from Class AAA Charlotte. — Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) August 25, 2026

Prior to tonight’s game vs. Texas, the Chicago White Sox placed outfielder Andrew Benintendi on the Bereavement/Family Medical Emergency List and recalled infielder/outfielder Rikuu Nishida from Class AAA Charlotte.

Regardless of what the masses may think, lefthander Anthony Kay has been solid for the Good Guys and is probably the second-best starter they currently have behind Sean Burke . Kay will make his 25th start of the season and has a 3.96 ERA and a 1.327 WHIP over 127 1/3 innings. He seems to keep improving, and in August alone, Kay has allowed just seven earned runs over 23 2/3 innings (four starts), good for a cool 2.66 ERA and a 2-1 record. If you ask me, his great outing against the Atlanta Braves last week went unrewarded because the offense was nowhere to be found.

Hopefully, the bats — or really anybody not named Miguel Vargas or Tristan Peters — can wake up to provide some early run support for Kay, but they will have a tough matchup with righthander Jacob deGrom on the mound. Peters has homered in three straight games, however, so let's see if he can make it four.

With Benintendi unavailable and a righty on the mound, Sam Antonacci is taking over as the DH and leading off today. Peters will shift to left field in Benintendi's place, while Brenton Doyle slots into center field and bats eighth. With those changes, today's lineup is almost identical to Monday's, and as we know, Will Venable loves the righty-lefty matchups. Still, I would be remiss not to mention Randal Grichuk 's career performance against deGrom: In 14 plate appearances, Grichuk has dominated. He's slashed .385/.429/1.000 with two home runs, amassing a 1.429 OPS.

deGrom is also making his 25th start of the season and holds a 3.77 ERA across 126 2/3 innings. The 38-year-old still has zero problems striking guys out and has rung up 157 batters this season. His 30.3% strikeout rate ranks in the top 8% of MLB pitchers. deGrom's fastball averages around 97 mph, though his off-speed pitches — slider, curveball and changeup — all fool batters, with all three pitches generating a whiff rate above 40%. His slider seems to be his most effective pitch, with opponents batting just .163 and slugging a measly .227 against it.

After being ejected from yesterday's game for heckling the ump, Joc Pederson will get another day off, with Justin Foscue remaining in the leadoff spot after a decent performance Monday. Corey Seager has been swinging a hot bat lately, and after two doubles and three RBIs yesterday, that is now apparent. In the past two weeks, Seager has the third-highest batting average in MLB (.419) and the sixth-highest OPS (1.164), and he's actually hit lefties better this year (.256 BA vs. .222 against righties).

First pitch is scheduled for 6:40 p.m. CDT, and it should be a beautiful night for a ballgame: 78º with partly cloudy skies. Watch on CHSN or listen on ESPN Chicago 1000 AM.

articles.title: Demetrius Fleming, 38, Found Hanging In Roanoke Rapids
articles.summary: An ongoing police investigation surrounds the death of a 38-year-old Black man found hanging last Friday morning. The police chief of the city reports that t...
articles.body:
An ongoing police investigation surrounds the death of a 38-year-old Black man found hanging last Friday morning. The police chief of the city reports that the cause of death is yet to be established.

The deceased man has been identified as Demetrius Eugene Fleming. Police Chief Lawrence Wiggins reported that police received a call just a little past 6:45 a.m. about a possible suicide case in the 1900 block of Roanoke Avenue. Fleming was discovered tied with a rope and declared dead at the scene.

According to Wiggins, Fleming was found dead when emergency personnel arrived at the house. Halifax County EMS and the Roanoke Rapids Fire Department were part of the effort. No information has been provided on the type of ligature used.

"We're treating this as an open, equivocal death investigation," Wiggins reported. This means that the cause of death is being investigated without making assumptions about whether it was a suicide, homicide, or accident. Wiggins stated that it would be premature to conclude and that the evidence would determine the cause of death.

At the afternoon press conference, Wiggins said that "anything is on the table" and detectives are exploring all angles of the case. When asked whether another person may be involved, he said everything is under consideration.

An autopsy is being carried out. According to Wiggins, the autopsy will provide the possibility to establish any other injuries on Fleming. Information should be available by Monday; however, it was not available by Tuesday.

According to Wiggins, police are aware of the case's history. He expressed his condolences to the family of Demetrius Fleming and added that they are cooperating with investigators since Friday.

The recent death case follows a similar incident that happened a week ago. Wiggins referred to the Raleigh case, where police ruled the death a suicide, according to WITN.

Chief Rico Boyce of Raleigh Police reported on Aug. 17 that video surveillance footage, along with traffic cameras, showed the 32-year-old man walking alone to the tree carrying an electrical cord, and investigators found no indication of anyone else's involvement. Boyce added that the woman's mother informed investigators of the man's mental problems.

The death of the 32-year-old man became an occasion of fear, pain, and concern for the population, according to the statement made by the North Carolina NAACP and its Raleigh-Apex branch.

The reason why the Raleigh death case received so much attention is the connection of a Black man found hanging from a tree in the South with the history of racist lynchings. Demetrius Eugene Fleming was originally from Roanoke Rapids, was born in January 1988, and his relatives said he was a husband and father.

Persons with information are encouraged to contact Halifax County Crime Stoppers at 252-583-4444 or via the P3 Tips app.

articles.title: Canadian man dies after being struck by a plane at Montreal airport
articles.summary: An airport worker at Montreal-Trudeau International Airport died after being struck by a plane.
articles.body:
An airport worker was struck and killed by a plane pushing back from the gate at Montreal-Trudeau International Airport Monday night after he reportedly tripped and fell on the tarmac.

According to Pax News , the aircraft was a French Bee Airbus A350 bound for Paris. About 7:30 p.m., the man, later identified by the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) as 39-year-old Oscar Robayo, was struck by the plane as it moved.

Radio-Canada spoke to a witness who said the man went under the plane and that people began screaming once they saw what was happening.

Robayo sustained what police described as "serious injuries" and was rushed to the hospital by emergency crews. He was later pronounced dead.

The IAM said Robayo was a ramp agent with Samsic Airport, a company that operates out of the airport providing passenger services and baggage handling. ADM Aéroports de Montréal, which operates the airport, issued a statement after the accident.

"The ADM Aéroports de Montréal team is deeply saddened by the loss of a member of the YUL airport community, an employee of Samsic, following an accident that occurred while carrying out their duties," the airport operator said.

The company added that assistance and support were being provided to employees and passengers who witnessed the accident. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada is investigating.

articles.title: Stevenage 0-3 Reading: Samba Rhythm Starts To Play
articles.summary: Jacob Brown, Paddy Lane and Randell Williams were on the scoresheet as Reading advanced to the third round of the League Cup.
articles.body:
"As the samba rhythm starts to play, dance with me, make me sway…"

So goes Paddy Lane 's chant. It's been sung out of optimism more than expectation in the year or so since he joined – the former Portsmouth winger struggling to show us what he's capable of on a consistent basis.

But tonight, at long last, this was absolutely Lane's night. It wasn't just about a single dramatic moment though, like when he netted winners last season over Port Vale or Bradford City. Rather, this was the kind of game that made you think that a big talent – one with so much potential to offer – may now have truly found his feet.

Would the Lane of last season have sent in that accurate low cross for Jacob Brown to convert for 1-0? Would he have cheekily lobbed Filip Marschall for 2-0? Football often comes down simply to being about confidence, and Lane demonstrated plenty of that throughout this evening's game.

But this was a pleasingly confident display all round from the Royals, who are now properly up and running for the season, and have a spot in the third round of the League Cup to look forward to. Although penalty shootout success is a victory of sorts, and we'd managed two of those already this season, tonight was Reading's first proper win.

And what better way to get it than in this kind of style? Three good goals from open play scored, none conceded (for the second match in a row) and a convincing attacking display that bore all the hallmarks of what Leam Richardson was trying to build over the summer: quick, direct and quality wide play.

The goals themselves were great examples of that. The first: a low cross from a winger (Lane setting up Brown). The second: a goal put away by a winger (Lane). The third: a winger putting the ball on a plate for another winger at the back post (Kyreece Lisbie, albeit playing up front in a 3-5-2, passing for Williams).

Not just a good performance then, but everything (as far as I can tell) going to plan. That samba rhythm wasn't confined just to Lane after all.

Richardson made nine changes from Saturday's 0-0 draw at AFC Wimbledon, with Joel Pereira and Benn Ward the only survivors. Conor Masterson and George Earthy were given full debuts, while there were also a number of first-team players included on a strong-looking bench.

Reading (4-2-3-1): Pereira; Ahmed, Masterson, Ward, Dorsett ; Fraser, Savage; Williams, Earthy, Lane; Brown Subs: Stevens, Roberts, Wing, Rinomhota, Stokes, Osho, Kyerewaa, Lisbie

Reading (4-2-3-1): Pereira; Ahmed, Masterson, Ward, Dorsett ; Fraser, Savage; Williams, Earthy, Lane; Brown

Subs: Stevens, Roberts, Wing, Rinomhota, Stokes, Osho, Kyerewaa, Lisbie

After a slightly shaky start in the early moments of the game, when debutant Masterson had to be on his toes, Reading took a 0-1 lead in the ninth minute. Liam Fraser pinged the ball out wide to Lane on the the left, whose low cross to the near post was diverted in by Brown.

The Royals played with confident at this point and looked to push for a second. The pairing down the right of full-back Ashqar Ahmed and winger Williams was a particularly potent-looking one, just as it had been in pre-season at Crawley Town.

A quarter of an hour or so after the opener, Reading doubled their lead. This time a long ball down the left wasn't dealt with properly by a Stevenage defender, whose loose header dropped for Lane. He still had a fair amount to do to beat the onrushing 'keeper, but dinked the ball over Marschall and home for 0-2 .

There was no other major action in the remainder of a positive half. The Royals generally looked bright in possession and did well enough to restrict a fairly limited attacking effort from the hosts, with Pereira not called into any heroics.

The second 45 was, on the whole, a much more even affair than the first, with the hosts coming fairly close to finding a way back into the game a few times.

That started off pretty early as Stevenage managed to put the Royals' defence under extended pressure soon after the restart. They even had the ball in the net not long after the interval, tucking it home from a deep free-kick on their left – but thankfully from an offside position.

Around 10 minutes later, more opportunities came Stevenage's way. Pereira did well to parry a powerful shot from the edge of the area on one occasion, and soon after watched a header (set up by a cross from our right) go wide of the post.

Down the other end though, Reading were carrying a threat going forwards of their own. This was a crucial difference from previous games this season, in which the Royals had looked good in the first half but struggled to maintain offensive consistency in the second.

The first example of that was a smart run in behind from Earthy a few minutes after the restart, getting on the edge of a Brown flicked header before forcing a save at the near post. The summer signing had other opportunities midway through the half – both of them being shots blocked inside the Stevenage area.

Reading seemed to be fading somewhat in the last 20 minutes, with the hosts in the ascendancy. The Royals' inability to kill the game off earlier in the half perhaps emboldened the home side, who piled more and more pressure on the visitors.

Richardson made his first change in the 81st minute, swapping Earthy off for Lisbie. That also meant a switch to a 3-5-2: Lane slotting in as a left-wing-back as the back four shunted over, with Williams going into midfield and Lisbie partnering Brown up front.

Ward then almost inadvertently helped Stevenage to halve the deficit. A low cross from Stevenage's left ricocheted off the defender inside the six-yard area, towards goal, but fortunately Pereira was able to block the ball.

Nervy times indeed, but Reading soon killed the game. Brown picked the ball up in space, slipped Lisbie in behind with a cute pass, and his low cross to the back post set up one of the easiest finishes Williams will have in his career. 0-3 , job done.

With the match killed off, Richardson made one more change. Lane was given a well deserved standing ovation from a jubilant away end as he was replaced by Daniel Kyerewaa – whose spot in the first team he could well soon take.

So, at the fifth time of asking, Reading finally have a normal-time win in 2026/27. What's more, we've got a mini cup run on our hands, and hopefully we'll have an exciting draw in the next round to look forward to.

Besides the obvious morale boost of a good performance and comfortable scoreline, Richardson will also be pleased with a few aspects of the Royals' performance: ruthlessness with chances, more consistent attacking threat across the 90 minutes, quality from out wide, not collapsing after the break, riding out the pressure Stevenage offered, and squad players staking a convincing claim to regular minutes in the league.

All in all then, surely exactly the kind of performance Richardson has been trying to establish in the last few months. The tricky next step: getting Reading to do this regularly in the league.

articles.title: Fake Bank Call Convinced Her to Open Her Safe. Police Say a Man Drove Off With $1.5 Million in Jewelry and Metals
articles.summary: A phone call from people posing as bank employees ended with a stranger driving into a Florida woman’s garage and leaving with approximately $1.5 million......
articles.body:
A phone call from people posing as bank employees ended with a stranger driving into a Florida woman's garage and leaving with approximately $1.5 million in jewelry and precious metals from her safe, according to police.

Treasure Island investigators say the scammers first convinced the older resident that her bank accounts and credit cards had been compromised. She wired approximately $280,000 before a bank employee recognized a second attempted transfer as suspicious and stopped it.

Police say the callers then changed tactics. They warned the woman that employees at her own bank could come to her home armed and steal her valuables, then offered a supposed way to protect them.

The six-month investigation has resulted in the arrests of James Arthur Graves Graham Jr., 24, and Alnesha Bianca Handy, 35, while authorities continue trying to identify other participants and locate missing property, according to National Jeweler .

The Callers Posed as Chase and Bank of America Employees

Treasure Island police responded to the woman's home on Feb. 10 after a report involving fraud, grand theft and burglary. Police Chief John Barkley said the callers claimed to represent Chase and Bank of America. When an actual bank employee stopped another large wire transfer, the people on the phone did not end the conversation.

FOX 13 reported that the callers instead convinced the woman that employees at her own bank were involved in the supposed criminal activity. Police say the woman remained on the phone for more than four and a half hours as the callers used fear and urgency to keep her following instructions. She eventually told them that her valuables were stored in a safe in her garage.

The callers instructed the woman to open the safe and garage door and then go back inside the house so she would not see the person supposedly coming to secure her valuables. Police say a vehicle entered the garage and the door was closed. The person inside emptied the safe and drove away with approximately $1.5 million in jewelry and precious metals.

License Plate Cameras and Fingerprints Led Police to Graham

Neighborhood surveillance and Treasure Island's Flock license plate reader system helped investigators narrow a description of the vehicle to a specific truck.

Police identified Graham as the person they believe went to the residence. He reported the vehicle stolen the following day, and investigators later recovered it in the Fort Lauderdale area.

Authorities said surveillance footage and latent fingerprints provided additional evidence. Treasure Island detectives then worked with Tampa police to search Graham's apartment, where investigators say they found clothing consistent with what the person at the victim's home had been wearing. Graham was arrested on one count of first-degree grand theft and one count of second-degree burglary.

The Wire Transfer Led Investigators to Georgia

Detectives and investigators with the Sixth Judicial Circuit State Attorney's Office spent months following financial records and leads through Tampa, Miami, Fort Lauderdale, Georgia, California and Texas. Investigators eventually traced part of the victim's wire transfer to a Georgia account they say belonged to Handy.

The Tampa Bay Times reported that the account, held under the name Handy Helping Hands LLC, contained $114,000 from the original transfer when investigators traced it.

Treasure Island investigators traveled to Georgia and interviewed Handy before the DeKalb County Sheriff's Office arrested her. Police said she faces a grand theft charge.

Police Recovered More Than 83% of the Wire Money

Investigators recovered more than 83% of the approximately $280,000 transferred electronically and returned it to the victim. Barkley described that level of recovery as highly unusual because fraud proceeds are often moved rapidly through multiple accounts and can become difficult to trace. Authorities believe the case may involve a larger fraud network, and additional arrests remain possible.

A Bank Will Not Send Someone to Your Home to Protect Your Valuables

An unexpected caller claiming a bank account has been compromised should be independently verified before any money or property is moved. Treasure Island police advise customers to hang up and call their financial institution using a trusted number, such as the one printed on the back of a bank card.

Banks will not instruct customers to hand jewelry, cash, gold or other valuables to a courier for safekeeping. They also will not require customers to move money to another account simply to protect it from fraud.

If someone claims a courier or representative is already on the way to a home, do not open the door or surrender property. Contact local law enforcement and the financial institution independently.

Anyone who has already sent a wire should notify the originating bank immediately and ask whether the transfer can be recalled or frozen. Acting quickly matters because stolen funds can move through additional accounts within hours.

articles.title: ‘No Conclusions’ Made as Investigation into Flight Attendant Mom’s Death During Layover Continues, Police Say
articles.summary: “Detectives are conducting numerous interviews, reviewing and recovering surveillance video, and examining evidence,” police said after Jenny Lupton’s death
articles.body:
Jenny Lupton, a Southwest Airlines flight attendant, was found dead in Hawaii last week

Her family previously said authorities told them that she appeared to have fallen from the hotel's balcony, but an investigation into her death remains open

"At this time, no conclusions have been made regarding the manner of death," police said in a statement released on Monday, Aug. 24

The family of Jenny Lupton, the Southwest flight attendant found dead during a layover in Hawaii last week, continues to wait for answers about her death.

In a news release shared with PEOPLE on Monday, Aug. 24, the Honolulu Police Department said their unattended death investigation began in Waikiki on Thursday, Aug. 20.

"The HPD Homicide Detail is actively investigating the circumstances surrounding her death and is working closely with her family," police said. "At this time, no conclusions have been made regarding the manner of death."

"This is a thorough investigation that will take time," police continued. "Detectives are conducting numerous interviews, reviewing and recovering surveillance video, and examining evidence as part of the investigative process."

Lupton, 50, of Moore, Okla., worked as a flight attendant for 29 years and was also a mom of one, according to NBC affiliate KFOR and CBS affiliate KWTV .

Family members said the Honolulu Department of the Medical Examiner contacted them, stating that Lupton appeared to have fallen from a 24th-floor balcony at her Waikiki hotel.

Her sister Tresa told KWTV that a hotel employee found Lupton's body, while KFOR reported the discovery was made on Aug. 20.

When reached for comment by PEOPLE, a spokesperson for the medical examiner's office said that the cause and manner of Lupton's death have not been determined, noting that a final determination could take several months.

Lupton was in Hawaii for work but was planning to stay for several days before returning, according to her family.

Tresa recalled receiving a text from Lupton, who had just gotten a new tattoo, hours before she was found dead. "She just went out with one of her flight attendant friends, and they danced and had a good time," Tresa said during an interview with KWTV.

Hannah Lupton, Jenny's niece, told USA Today that the family does not believe their loved one died by suicide and "are worried that there is possible foul play involved."

In a statement shared with PEOPLE on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Oklahoma Attorney General said their "office is in contact with Hawaii Attorney General Anne Lopez's office to help ensure a proper investigation into Jenny Lupton's death."

"We are also in contact with the Lupton family who deserve to have answers about this tragedy," the spokesperson added.

Southwest Airlines has also offered their "condolences and support" and says they "are engaged with local authorities as they investigate."

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

Honolulu Police have said that in order to preserve the integrity of the investigation, authorities "will limit the release of certain information while the investigation remains ongoing."

"On behalf of Jenny Lupton's family, we ask for patience as detectives conduct this investigation and respectfully request that the family's privacy be honored during this difficult time," the department added.

Additionally, authorities asked the public to refrain from sharing unverified information.

Meanwhile, a GoFundMe created for Lupton's family has raised over $11,000 as of Tuesday afternoon.

articles.title: IndyCar’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix Promoter: ‘This Is My Sistine Chapel’
articles.summary: IndyCar's Freedom 250 Grand Prix Of Washington DC was an epic spectacle in the Nation's Capital. Forbes Sports Money provides a behind-the-scenes look at the...
articles.body:
There is a slogan in auto racing that best exemplifies the unbelievable 60-year success of Team Penske and Roger Penske's incredible accomplishments in business.

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington DC was a perfect example of that slogan because Penske and IndyCar were able to create a sporting event in the National Mall of Washington, DC that was so stunning, so magical, and so well-orchestrated that it is hard to put it into words to someone who wasn't on the grounds.

It was the first auto racing ever held on the historic streets that surround the National Mall. Penske Corporation President Bud Denker was the man responsible for taking an impossible task and turning it into a moment of pride for IndyCar, the 150,000 spectators and 3,282,000 viewers that watched on FOX.

"I've never been on a journey like this in my life," Denker told me after the race. "I've been in a lot of deals, been in a lot of decisions. Been in a lot of sponsorship deals that were incredibly big, but I just can't ever imagine doing anything bigger than this.

"The Sistine Chapel was probably the most amazing thing that happened for Leonardo da Vinci.

Freedom 250 Grand Prix Gets Biggest Viewership For A Non-Indy 500 in Decades

It was the most-viewed non-Indy 500 race since the start of the IndyCar Series when the Indy Racing League and Champ Car merged before the 2008 season. It was up 364 percent over last year's 708,000 viewers for the FOX portion of last year's 15 th race from Portland, when the first 31 minutes started on FS1.

Sunday's viewership was up 279 percent with last year's 867,000 viewers for Sunday non-Indy 500 races on FOX.

The race partially overlapped with the NASCAR Cup race from New Hampshire which ran on USA from 2:14-6:36 pm.

The full race telecast averaged 1,686,000 viewers and the race peaked with 3,482,000 viewers from 2:30-2:45pm.

IndyCar on FOX is averaging 1,875,000 viewers through 15 races, up 32 percent vs. last year's season to date of 1,416,000 and up 70 percent over the 2024 season to date when 1,106,000 for races on NBC/USA/CNBC.

It was IndyCar's gift to the 250 th Birthday of the United States, but the positive reaction from those that came from around the world to witness the race may be IndyCar's biggest gift. Many of those fans had never attended an auto race before. Some left the race saying they were now IndyCar fans.

Freedom 250 On Track Action Driving Reaction

From a racing standpoint, Kyle Kirkwood dominated, winning the race after leading 128 laps of the 147-lap contest. There was plenty of action, though, throughout the field with 155 passes during the contest.

"It was racy. You could pass," said third-place finisher Will Power of Andretti Global. "A lot of my positions were gained just on-track passes. It was everything you'd want. Having an American President here watching the whole race, still there when I pulled up on the grid, you could see President Trump still watching, which meant that the race must have been pretty engaging, which is really good stuff. Great for the series."

I asked Power had what point in the day the moment of the magnitude of this spectacle hit him?

"Probably when we jumped in the truck and drove around," Power said. "You see the pageantry. It had a very Indy 500 vibe.

"I think IndyCar is in the best shape it's ever been in since I've been in the series. That's 21 years. It's just progressively gone up. More recently it's taken a big step. Really proud to be a part of it."

While some fans may look at the same driver leading 128 laps in front of the field with a negative reaction, the value of this event wasn't necessarily what happened on the track, it was having IndyCar as the star attraction for a huge crowd in a setting unlike any other.

It wasn't the Indianapolis 500, where 350,000 fans jam the Indianapolis Motor Speedway for the world's most famous and historic race. But for a street race near the end of the summer celebrating a milestone moment in the history of the United States that drew 150,000 enthusiastic fans, it was a major event for both IndyCar and the USA.

"This morning when I woke up, quite honestly, there's an instinct that you have when you wake up and your heart is already racing," the race-winner said. "I only get that one other place, and that's the Indy 500. Just that sensation, it gives it its own energy. That's what this place had.

"This was a very special day. We were very prepared for it. Outside of the Indy 500, I don't think there's another race that you'd want to win."

Freedom 250 Grand Prix One Last Celebration Of The 250th Birthday Of The United States

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, DC was historic for where it was being held. The US Capitol Building in the background behind the flag stand and other iconic structures such as the National Archives, the Washington Monument, the National Archives and other famed attractions made it a spectacular setting.

Every branch of the United States Military was honored with each branch's marching band performing on the track. There were seven military flyovers during the event including the B2 Stealth Bomber and a special flyover from Air Force One escorted by F-15 Eagles and F-15 Fighting Falcons.

Freedom 250 Grand Prix Was IndyCar's American Dream

Denker and his team were able to create a spectacle out of something many critics didn't believe would ever happen. He started a lengthy lobbying effort that began in August 2025 with 81 meetings on Capitol Hill trying to get it approved by the United States House of Representatives and US Senate.

On January 21, the project was at an impasse. There wasn't enough support to get approval for the areas of the National Mall that were required to put up a temporary street circuit.

Denker told Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy that he was pulling the plug, that the race wouldn't happen. Duffy encouraged Denker to hold off because he had another plan.

He was able to get an Executive Order from President Donald J. Trump on January 30.

That's when the hard work began to plan the event, and secure the proper permits and licenses required because of all the different jurisdictions involved.

"If you asked anybody in this town, or I would say on our industry, could we have a race in Washington, D.C. a year ago, the answer would have been, 'are you crazy?'" Denker told me. "That is what most of them said when I first came up here a year ago.

"But I didn't think it was a crazy idea.

"Resiliency, I think, is the key word for me. Persistence is the other piece. And don't take no, because there are a lot of 'no's' here.

"People have this phrase, 'Penske Perfect.' We're never perfect, but we're not going to have people think we are. That's pretty good to me, and many people thought this was perfect. And for a first -time event, my team made a flawless execution."

Although he is the Penske Corporation President and works out of the corporate offices near Detroit, Denker spent most of his time living in Washington, DC beginning last August. He was running solo until March, trying to put the event together.

"Remember, my team also had to do the IndyCar race at Arlington as a first-time event in March," Denker explained. "Jonathan Bailey was running the operations at Arlington and then they had to do the Chevrolet Detroit Grand Prix in June, so I was borrowing resources wherever I could.

"Most of it was me initially to get the organization to meet all the people, all the stakeholders I had to meet with. 50-plus stakeholders that surround this track, multiple meetings, greasing the skids before these guys got here."

Freedom 250 Work Kicked Into High Gear In June

Denker said it the race was really put together with his full team beginning in June, which meant it had to be ready to go in a little over two full months.

"It's an interesting city because we're in John Hopkins University right now, but the sidewalk outside is owned by the National Park Service," Denker explained. "The curb across the street is owned by the National Art Gallery, and the street is owned by the city of Washington, DC. Down about 50 yards, that area is owned by the National Archives. Further up the road, that walkway is owned by the Smithsonian Institute.

"And then you have all of the Capitol grounds. We can't touch the Capitol on the curb, because that would violate the president's executive order.

"All of these entities, we had to deal with to put things together, 1,350 pages it permits. To weld a manhole cover here, you need a big, big, big, thick page of permits. We couldn't wash the track here like we do everywhere else. We couldn't wash the track because we couldn't wash water into the drainage areas here, despite the fact that rain goes down those drainage areas as well.

"So those are just complexities that you have to do here. But despite that, we got through it all, and we have great partnerships with the city, and 1,350 pages of permits is a lot."

Denker was all over the property leading up to the race and rode in one of the Presidential Limousines on a ceremonial lap. Afterwards, Denker and Penske watched the contest in the Presidential Suite along with the President and First Lady.

Could The Freedom 250 Grand Prix Return to Washington DC In The Future?

President Trump, Washington, DC Mayor Muriel Bowser and many other government officials want the Freedom 250 Grand Prix to be back on the IndyCar schedule in future years. But this race was originally created as a one-time-only event to help celebrate the 250 th birthday of the United States.

The Penske Corporation invested $35 million to make this event happen. Although 150,000 fans came on Sunday with 214,000 fans for the two-day weekend, tickets were free and distributed through a lottery system from the 288,000 requests that were submitted.

Revenue came from the sale of lavish VIP suites and from an impressive list of corporation sponsors. Merchandise sales were impressive with lines of spectators buying up all the Freedom 250 Grand Prix merchandise they could find. According to Denker, $900,000 of merchandise was sold on Saturday alone. At the Grand Prix of Arlington, $900,000 of merchandise was sold over the weekend for a first-time event.

For it to become an annual event, the business structure would have to generate significant revenue.

"We have a difficult choice to make," Denker said. "The question is this. How many people would come back again for the event in Year Two, a non-anniversary year for the United States? Could you charge tickets, a price for tickets, to cover some of the revenue and the loss you have because this is so expensive? Is it $50 a person? What would that do to the crowd?

"Or did you tease them enough this year enough this year that they really would want to come back and would come back also by paying something that's reasonable?

"That's the questions we have to look at. And I think the key thing for us is to probably talk to our sponsors and say, is there interest in coming back?

"But ultimately, it's a Roger Penske decision. We'll make that decision pretty soon."

Denker sat with Penske and his wife, Kathy, in the Presidential Suite throughout the race and expressed his appreciation and gratitude for what the event meant to him and his family.

"This is my crowning achievement," Denker said. "Roger has had a lot of crowning achievements in his life, many more than I have, but it won't get better for me. I know this is one of the top ones for Roger."

This event was about Patriotism, and the fans that came to the race were happy to be part of the celebration and turned the National Mall into one of the "happiest places on Earth" at least for one day.

Roger Penske Thanks Freedom 250 Fans With A Special Full-Page Letter In The Washington Post

Penske showed his appreciation to the fans by taking out a full-page ad in The Washington Post on Tuesday with the following letter:

"To Our Fans, Thank you for making the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C., such an extraordinary and memorable event for our nation.

"The energy and enthusiasm you brought to our nation's capital made this weekend truly special. Whether you joined us in Washington or watched from home, your passion for INDYCAR and motorsports was on full display and helped create a celebration worthy of America's 250th anniversary.

"We are grateful to President Trump and his Administration for their leadership and support in making this historic event possible. We also thank Mayor Bowser and the broader team in Washington, D.C., for their partnership and for working together with our organization to bring the Freedom 250 Grand Prix to life in our Nation's Capital.

"The Freedom 250 Grand Prix brought together the speed, competition and pageantry of INDYCAR racing with an incredible celebration of our country. Seeing the cars race through Washington, surrounded by iconic landmarks and thousands of fans, created images and memories that will stay with all of us for years to come.

"I also want to thank all of our INDYCAR drivers and teams for delivering an outstanding weekend of competition and congratulate Kyle Kirkwood on his victory in the Freedom 250 Grand Prix.

"Motorsports has always been about more than the cars on the track. It is about the fans, the teams, the drivers, our partners and the many people behind the scenes who make our sport possible. This weekend was a tremendous example of what can be accomplished when people come together around a shared vision.

"Our partners at FOX played an important role in bringing that experience to millions of viewers across the country. Their commitment to INDYCAR has helped showcase our drivers, teams and racing to a growing audience, and we are proud to have them as a partner.

"We are also grateful to the many brands and partners whose support helped make this historic event possible, including Monumental Sports & Entertainment and Harbinger. Their commitment and collaboration were instrumental in bringing this ambitious vision to life.

"As we celebrate America's 250th anniversary, all of us at INDYCAR are incredibly proud to have played a part in this historic occasion.

"Most importantly, thank you again to our fans. Your passion is what drives our sport forward, and we could not be prouder to have shared this unforgettable celebration of America and INDYCAR with you.
