articles.title: US spy chief visits Russia for meetings, media reports
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, U.S. media outlets reporte...
articles.body:
A C-17 Globemaster, believed to be carrying U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, lands near Riga, Latvia

WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, U.S. media outlets reported, citing unnamed sources.

The ‌trip would be the first known visit to the Russian capital by a ‌U.S. spy chief since Ratcliffe's predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Vladimir Putin in November 2021. About three months ​after that meeting, the Russian president launched Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.

CBS News and Axios reported the visit by Ratcliffe, U.S. President Donald Trump's CIA chief, who served as director of national intelligence in Trump's first term. The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what ‌the talks are expected to ⁠cover.

The CIA declined to comment. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov neither confirmed nor denied the report, telling Reuters President Vladimir Putin did not plan to ⁠have a meeting with Ratcliffe.

The U.S. last week asked Ukraine not to launch air strikes around Moscow, St. Petersburg, and some northern territories of Russia on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of this week ​because ​a plane carrying a senior U.S. official would ​be flying to the Russian capital, ‌said a source familiar with the matter.

The source declined to provide further information. The Financial Times first reported the U.S. message to Ukraine.

On Monday, the U.S. warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, a move aimed at stepping up economic pressure on Tehran to settle the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February.

The U.S. has no ‌ambassador to Russia, which maintains a close strategic partnership ​with Iran involving extensive military, economic and diplomatic ties.

Tehran ​supplied Moscow with drones for its ​war against Ukraine. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy accused Russia of ‌supplying its version of those drones to ​Iran.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment ​reported by Reuters in April said that Russia has aided Iran with satellite imagery for use in targeting U.S. facilities in the Middle East.

Moscow denies providing such assistance ​and has said it ‌is ready to help resolve the U.S.-Iran conflict.

(Reporting by Daphne Psaledakis and Jonathan Landay; ​additional reporting by Vladimir Soldatkin in Moscow and Dan Flynn. Writing by ​Susan Heavey; editing by Chizu Nomiyama, Jekaterina Golubkova)

articles.title: 5-foot red-tailed boa constrictor found crossing rural road in Canada
articles.summary: Boas are known "escape artists," able to slip through surprisingly small gaps.
articles.body:
A 5-foot red-tailed boa constrictor found crossing a rural road in Ontario left everyone wondering where exactly it came from.

According to GuelphToday , Katherine Leonard, senior manager of community services at the Guelph Humane Society (GHS), said the humane society received a call from a resident after a large snake was seen on the road in Arthur near Eliza Street and Wells Street.

Before that call reached staff, another person in the community had already secured the animal in a large plastic container with duct tape, which was how it arrived at GHS.

The humane society does not usually handle animal control in the Arthur area, but staff still assisted in this special instance and pulled an old enclosure from storage, specifically saved for this type of situation.

During intake, Leonard said, the boa showed no immediate signs of illness or injury and appeared to be a fully grown adult measuring just over 5 feet long.

She added that the snake likely had not been outdoors for long and had "been previously cared for," indicating captivity rather than a wild animal encounter.

VCA Canada says red-tailed boas — also called common boas — are nonvenomous snakes from Central and South America that can grow to about 13 feet and often live 20 to 30 years. They are also strong climbers and require tall, secure enclosures in captivity.

Leonard said the humane society does occasionally receive surrendered ball pythons, but a snake of this size is unusual. "It's definitely one of the larger snakes we've seen here," she said.

Leonard noted that boas are known "escape artists," able to slip through surprisingly small gaps in doors, windows, and even ceiling tiles. She said another possible explanation is that the snake may have been dumped by someone who could no longer afford or handle its care.

Large snakes require space, specialized housing, and a long-term commitment — all of which can create serious challenges for owners and rescue organizations.

The snake is being held under the humane society's standard impound process. Leonard said the shelter will keep it through the required five-day period, after which it could be made available for adoption if no owner comes forward.

The shelter is also asking people who are missing a snake — or who know of one that has gone missing — to contact GHS.

Animals that can live for decades and require specialized habitats can quickly become difficult to care for when their needs are underestimated. When that happens, the consequences reach beyond a single household, affecting neighbors, rescuers, and the animal itself.

"It was crossing the road, so it's very fortunate it didn't succumb to any injuries," Leonard said. "Our hope with any animal is always to reunite it with its owner, but, in the event that it doesn't, that's what we're here for."

"I am not taking back a single thing. Maybe I could have said it nicer. Maybe I could have been more diplomatic," Finebaum said . "I didn't know a single Indiana graduate until midway through last season, and now they are literally falling out of Amazon trucks. I don't know what's going on here."

"I think Indiana is a really good team. I predicted they'll go to the playoffs. They're probably 10-2. I'm worried about their offensive line," Finebaum said. "Worried about the secondary. Worried about the quarterback. Yes, the schedule, which I went into.

articles.title: Wood fire prompts evacuations in Riverside County
articles.summary: A fire in an incoporated area of Perris has prompted evacuation orders and warnings, authorities said.
articles.body:
A fire in Riverside County has prompted evacuation orders and warnings in the Inland Empire.

The Wood fire was burning near Orland and Roth roads in an unincorporated portion of Perris, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. It comes amid an extreme heat warning in many parts of Southern California, including in the valleys of San Bernardino and Riverside counties, for "dangerously hot conditions" with high temperatures up to 110 degrees.

The fire had burned about 60 acres as of 3 p.m. and is 0% contained, according to Cal Fire.

At 4:30 p.m., there were road closures on Salter Road at Fox Street, and at Juniper Road and Ida Leona Road.

Nearly 170 personnel have been deployed to respond to the fire, including three helicopters and 29 engines, Cal Fire said.

Officials issued evacuation orders for zones RVC-1060 and RVC-1059 shortly after 2 p.m., warning of "immediate threat to life." The evacuation area is bounded roughly by Orange Avenue to the north, Juniper Road to the west, Santa Rosa Mine Road and San Jacinto Avenue to the south and Old Elsinore Road to the east. An evacuation map can be found here .

Evacuees, and their pets, can go to the Perris Library at 163 E. San Jacinto Ave. for shelter and other resources, according to the order.

Officials also issued evacuation warnings for surrounding neighborhoods. The cause of the fire is under investigation, and it was not immediately known if there had been civilian injuries or structural damage.

Most of Harford Springs Reserve, a park featuring several hiking trails, is under an evacuation warning, according to the map. The northwestern part of Motte Rimrock Reserve, a biological field station on a rocky plateau managed by UC Riverside, also falls in an evacuation warning zone.

The blaze was reported just before 1 p.m. near the area of Rider Street and Dreamglo Lane, Cal Fire/Riverside County Fire Department posted on X. The fire was, at the time, burning at a "dangerous rate in medium grass and brush."

By 2:15 p.m., the agency said the fire was burning at a "moderate rate."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Instagram chief admits touting teen safety tool while omitting it was barely used
articles.summary: Adam Mosseri, who oversees Instagram at Meta, admitted in a California court on Tuesday that he touted newly launched safety tools for teens without disclosi...
articles.body:
Adam Mosseri, who oversees Instagram at Meta, admitted in a California court on Tuesday that he touted newly launched safety tools for teens without disclosing low adoption rates from early testing several years ago.

With more than three billion users around the world, Meta is fending off accusations by a coalition of 29 US states that it deliberately designed its products to hook children and gather their data while misleading the public.

The trial entered its second week on Monday and is expected to last through late September.

A lawyer with the Colorado Attorney General's office, Jason Slothouber, questioned Mosseri about the low usage of the tools, known as Take a Break and Quiet Mode, which were launched in 2021 and 2023, respectively.

Other witnesses have testified over the past week that these tools weren't effective, though Mosseri pushed back on the idea that adoption remains low.

"This is one feature with a disappointingly low usage rate which since this time has significantly improved," Mosseri said.

On December 8, 2021, Mosseri testified at a Congressional hearing about the negative impacts of social media on young people. One day before, Meta published a blog post, authored by Mosseri, about rolling out new safety features for teens.

"Early test results show that once teens set the reminders, more than 90% of them keep them on," the blog post says.

However, that number referred to the number of people who kept it on after turning it on.

When asked if Meta disclosed its low adoption, which only reached 1 or 2 percent of the accounts, Mosseri admitted the company did not but said the safety features were later turned on by default in Teen Accounts, which have parental controls and launched in 2024.

However, Mosseri couldn't recall if Meta had ever disclosed the percentage of teen accounts that have parental controls turned on.

Mosseri will continue testifying on Wednesday. Founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg is also expected to testify, though it's unclear when.

Meta knew that its tools for protecting teenagers on Instagram were largely ineffective, other witnesses have testified.

Internal Meta documents shown to jurors on Tuesday said that Take a Break, which allows users to set reminders to stop scrolling, reached an adoption rate of 1.8 percent, while Quiet Mode, which silences late-night notifications, reached 8.7 percent.

Under questioning from state lawyers, Francesco Fogu, Meta's director of product design at Instagram, said Tuesday that he was not aware of the numbers, but conceded that the company "knew adoption rates would be lower" if those tools were not turned on by default.

Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who will decide the case using the jury's verdict as guidance, appeared stunned that Fogu was unaware of the internal data.

If Meta is convicted, US states will seek around $200 billion in penalties, and a court loss could force fundamental changes to its business model and send shockwaves through the industry.

Two former employees also testified that Take a Break and Quiet Mode were not effective.

"In my experience, Take a Break is a feature that's designed to fail," Arturo Bejar, a former Meta engineering director, testified last week.

George Volichenko, a data scientist who worked on safety features at Instagram in 2022 and 2023, said Monday that adoption rates for those features were "very low and disappointing" and just "a drop in the ocean."

He painted Meta's leadership as uninterested in meaningfully boosting their use.

Leadership did not approve turning on Quiet Mode by default for younger teens, which held down adoption because the setting was hard to find in the app, Volichenko said.

Switching the safety features on by default would have caused a "notable negative impact" on user engagement, he said.

Meta's business model revolves around selling advertising, and the company earns more when users spend more time on its apps.

articles.title: N.J. restaurant writes ‘happy wheelchair birthday’ on disabled customer’s dessert. Here’s what we know.
articles.summary: A birthday celebration ended with an unsettling message.
articles.body:
A birthday dinner at an upscale New Jersey restaurant took an unexpected turn when dessert arrived at the table with an insensitive message.

Antonia Sinibaldi , a Hudson County native who suffered a spinal injury in a car crash when she was 2 years old, spent her 29th birthday at Blu on the Hudson back in June with her friends and family.

When Sinibaldi's dessert arrived at the table, next to a lit candle was a message written in icing: "happy wheelchair birthday!"

"It took me by surprise," Sinibaldi, who has relied on a motorized wheelchair and ventilator for most of her life, told CBS News . "I shouldn't be reminded of something that I already know."

The Weehawken resident told CBS News she asked management for an explanation, but was unsatisfied with their response.

"He offered to send me more drinks, more drinks, more drinks," Sinibaldi told CBS News. "What good will that do?"

Sinibaldi declined comment at time of publishing. Messages left for Blu on the Hudson were not returned.

In a statement given to CBS News, Blu on the Hudson apologized for the incident.

"We at Blu on the Hudson are aware of the recent video circulating on social media, and we are deeply saddened by what occurred. We sincerely apologize to the guest and to everyone who was hurt or offended by this incident which took place on June 20, 2026. Treating every guest with dignity, respect, and care is fundamental to who we are as a company."

The statement went on to provide further context for the incident, noting Blu on the Hudson's staff uses tables and seat numbers to identify where dishes are delivered. "Wheelchair" was used as a reference for where the birthday dessert with a candle was to be delivered, but was not intended to be written on the plate.

"There was absolutely no malicious or disrespectful intent behind the notation," the statement read. "However, we fully understand how seeing that word written on a plate could be deeply hurtful and upsetting."

Blu on the Hudson also said in the statement it has since talked to the staff about the importance of proper ticketing and communication, in hopes of making sure an incident like this doesn't happen again. The restaurant said it also unsuccessfully attempted to reconnect with Sinibaldi to apologize further.

articles.title: Former news anchor pleads guilty to stabbing mother to death on Halloween
articles.summary: Angelynn Mock pleaded guilty to first-degree murder after allegedly believing her mother Anita Avers was the devil during the Halloween stabbing.
articles.body: A former Missouri television news anchor has admitted to fatally stabbing her mother on Halloween last year after apparently believing she was the devil, authorities said last week. Angelynn "Angie" Mock, 48, pleaded guilty to one count of first-degree murder in connection with the slaying of her mother, 80-year-old Anita Avers, on Oct. 31, 2025, the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office announced Friday. Under the terms of the plea, Mock faces life in prison with eligibility for parole after 25 years. FLORIDA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING MOM AND BURNING BODY BECAUSE SHE ‘WANTED TO BE CREMATED’ Officers were called to the Wichita home Mock and Avers shared with Mock's stepfather around 7:50 a.m. on Oct. 31. When they arrived, Mock was found outside with cuts on her hands, according to the Wichita Police Department. Avers was taken to a hospital with multiple stab wounds, and later died. Mock made several statements indicating she believed her mother was the devil, according to a probable cause affidavit. She allegedly told authorities that she killed her mother to "save herself." Mock's stepfather told KAKE-TV that she had been diagnosed with mental illness and suffered from delusions and depression. FORMER TV ANCHOR ACCUSED OF KILLING HER MOTHER RULED INCOMPETENT, MURDER CASE PUT ON HOLD She previously worked as a news anchor and reporter for Fox 2 in St. Louis from 2011 to 2015, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to that, she worked as a morning anchor from 2007 to 2011 at KOKH-TV in Oklahoma City, the profile states. Mock held other reporting stints in Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska. articles.title: His Clinics Billed Medicaid More Than $36 Million in Six Months. A Plea Deal Calls for 15 Years in Prison
articles.summary: A Yuma doctor accused of using medical businesses he controlled to bill Arizona’s Medicaid program more than $36 million in a matter of months could... Read...
articles.body:
A Yuma doctor accused of using medical businesses he controlled to bill Arizona's Medicaid program more than $36 million in a matter of months could spend 15 years in prison under a proposed plea agreement filed in his criminal case.

Dr. Irfan Fazil, 54, founder of Bio Family Clinic, is accused of operating a racketeering enterprise that defrauded the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, known as AHCCCS, between July 2025 and May 2026.

Investigators say three AHCCCS-enrolled provider businesses controlled by Fazil and his spouse submitted more than $36 million in claims between July and December 2025 alone. The billing included tens of thousands of X-rays, more than 10,000 ultrasounds and more than 1,000 ECGs, according to KYMA .

The case took a major turn Aug. 25 when a plea agreement was filed calling for a 15-year prison sentence. Fazil has not yet formally entered the plea in court.

Patients Said They Never Received Some of the Services Billed

Court records reviewed by KYMA said the three provider entities' AHCCCS billing during the final six months of 2025 represented approximately 97% of their revenue for that year.

Investigators then compared the claims with information from patients. Multiple people said they never received services billed under their names, while some were outside Arizona or even outside the United States on dates when the records indicated treatment occurred.

The volume of diagnostic procedures also drew scrutiny, including the tens of thousands of X-rays, more than 10,000 ultrasounds and more than 1,000 ECGs cited in the probable-cause records.

The State Accused Him of Operating a Racketeering Enterprise

The case became part of Arizona's participation in the 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown. The Arizona Attorney General's Office said Fazil was charged with fraudulent schemes and artifices, illegal control of an enterprise, theft, conspiracy and drug-related felonies.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise operated from July 2025 through May 2026 and that Fazil conspired with another person to commit money laundering and theft. Bio Family Clinic was separately charged with fraudulent schemes and artifices.

The Proposed Deal Calls for 15 Years in Prison

Under the agreement filed Aug. 25, Fazil would receive a 15-year prison sentence for fraud, illegal control of an enterprise and theft, KYMA reported .

The proposed deal calls for conspiracy and possession of dangerous drugs charges to be dismissed. It would also require Fazil to give up his medical license and Drug Enforcement Administration registration. Another provision requires Fazil to provide authorities with passwords to his cellphones and laptops.

Fazil remains in the Yuma County Detention Center on a $50 million bond. Although the written agreement has been filed, KYMA reported Aug. 25 that he had not yet formally entered the plea before a judge.

His next court appearance is scheduled for Sept. 4. Until the plea is entered and accepted, the proposed 15-year disposition is not a final sentence.

Patients Can Report Medical Services They Never Received

Medical billing fraud can sometimes be detected by the people whose identities appear on claims, particularly when records show appointments, tests or procedures that never occurred.

The AHCCCS Office of Inspector General specifically identifies billing for services or supplies that were never provided, double billing, overbilling and incorrect coding as examples of potential provider fraud.

AHCCCS members who notice an unfamiliar service should compare the information with their own medical records and contact their health plan or provider for clarification. Dates when the patient was elsewhere, procedures the patient does not recognize or repeated services that never occurred should not simply be ignored.

Suspected provider fraud can be reported directly to AHCCCS OIG. The agency says anyone may make a report and that reports may be submitted anonymously.

I looked at him like, 'Did you really just say that?' Here is a guy who is incredibly smart, runs a hedge fund, and has an MBA from a top business school, and he honestly thought in Mexico they spoke Mexican. I was dumbfounded."

5. "Bank debit cards were a fairly new concept. I got an overdraft notice from the bank. My ex-husband said it was no problem, we could just go to the ATM and withdraw money to deposit in our checking account. 9. "My husband and I were discussing our neighbor, who just got diagnosed with prostate cancer, and my husband said that he should probably get his prostate examined. articles.body:
Steve Kerr will have a former Arizona guard under his tutelage this NBA season.

Brandon Williams has signed a one-year, $2.6 million contract with the Golden State Warriors , ESPN's Shams Charania reported Tuesday.

Free agent guard Brandon Williams has agreed to a one-year, $2.6 million deal to sign with the Golden State Warriors, agents Derek Lafayette and Curtis Lawrence tell ESPN. Williams averaged 13 points, 3.9 assists and 22.2 minutes per night across 66 games for Dallas last season. pic.twitter.com/VcDytjCDKe — Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) August 25, 2026

Williams averaged 13 points, 3.9 assists and 22.2 minutes per night across 66 games for Dallas last season. pic.twitter.com/VcDytjCDKe

The former Wildcats point guard is coming off a career-best season with Dallas Mavericks in which he averaged 13 points and 3.9 assists in 22 minutes per game. Williams appeared in 66 games with Dallas after spending the previous two seasons on two-way deals.

The 26-year-old debuted with Portland in 2021 after going undrafted out of college. Williams missed his sophomore season at Arizona due to a knee injury and spent the following year preparing for a professional career.

Williams, a Los Angeles native, is heading back to his home state to play for a Warriors franchise that has fallen on hard times in recent years. Williams will compete with De'Anthony Melton for the backup point guard role behind Stephen Curry .

Williams is the third former Wildcat to play under Kerr in Golden State, joining Andre Iguodala and Nico Mannion .

articles.title: L.A. takes aim at phenibut, an unregulated 'gas station drug' that is growing in popularity
articles.summary: L.A. City Council hopes to regulate phenibut, a drug one councilmember says is widely available to children in gas stations and convenience stores.
articles.body:
Los Angeles is looking to regulate another "gas station drug" on commercial shelves.

In a unanimous vote Tuesday, the L.A. City Council instructed the City Attorney to draft new regulations for phenibut, a Cold War-era drug that is said to have been used by Soviet cosmonauts, but abused now as a central nervous system depressant.

Regulations will include restricting sales to people under 21, banning sales near schools and daycare centers and the creation of labels warning against its use, according to the motion .

The full council must vote again on ordinance language before the regulations become law.

"Phenibut is a powerful, unregulated substance that has been sold openly to kids at gas stations and convenience stores across our city, with no age restrictions and little warning of its risks. That ends now," said Councilmember Heather Hutt, who authored the motion.

Nina Paquette, a Marlborough High School senior, brought the existence of the drug and its dangers to Hutt's attention.

"The drug is often marketed directly to children, who are able to purchase it easily without any age restrictions," Hutt said. "Our young people are at extreme risk of developing a severe dependence on this easily accessible substance."

Phenibut is not federally regulated and cannot be legally sold as a dietary supplement. Despite that, Hutt said, it's easily available in L.A. convenience stores.

Paquette, a former intern for state Assemblymember John Harabedian (D-Pasadena), said phenibut pills are often marketed as "smart drugs" or "brain boosters" on social media.

"Teenagers can buy it at gas stations with no idea it can cause addiction, seizures, hallucinations, psychosis and coma," Paquette said.

In Russia, phenibut is a prescription drug used to treat anxiety, insomnia, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and other ailments. It functions much like Valium or Xanax by depressing the central nervous system, and has been banned in several countries and Utah .

According to some studies , phenibut can be addictive and cause withdrawal symptoms. Studies looking into poison control reports found it can lead to trouble breathing , coma or death. Researchers warn that it is an up-and-coming drug that western medicine knows little about.

It's not the first time an unregulated gas station drug has come under fire in L.A.

The Southeast Asian plant kratom and its alternate powerful synthetic alkaloid 7-OH, another drug that escaped federal regulation for years and regularly sold in gas stations and smoke shops, was linked to six overdose deaths across L.A. County last year.

Kratom was temporarily deemed a scheduled substance by the FDA and has been pulled from shelves across California , according to Governor Gavin Newsom.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Texas nature center rebuilt after Guadalupe flood, but Town Creek flood wrecked the interior again
articles.summary: "All of the new renovations from 2025 were damaged."
articles.body:
Rebuilding after one flood is difficult enough. At Texas' Riverside Nature Center, staff restored the historic Lawson Store after a 2025 flood linked to backflow from the Guadalupe River, only to see a 2026 flood rip through the interior all over again.

The Kerr County Lead reported that the floods were very different, according to Riverside Nature Center's executive director Becky Etzler. The 2025 event followed the more familiar pattern of Guadalupe River backflow, but the 2026 flooding came out of Town Creek, which she described as a "rampaging monster."

Although the structure remained intact, the interior work completed after the first disaster did not. "All of the new renovations from 2025 were damaged," Etzler said. "We had to virtually start again in the Lawson Store."

Riverside Nature Center began in 1994 under founder Susan Sander, a Wisconsin-born freelance photographer. Through volunteer effort and privately raised funds, the organization acquired three historic homesteads and developed them into a regional natural resource hub.

Staff naturalist China Rubiano now oversees surveys of birds, butterflies, and plants, monitors seasonal changes in native species, and cares for Shucks — the center's captive-bred corn snake.

A large shipping container being used for storage after the first flood broke loose from its foundation, drifted across the parking lot, and crashed into the children's music garden, damaging several instruments.

Yet when it came to a stop, the container was positioned to shield the center's new 20,000-gallon rainwater-harvesting tank, which The Kerr County Lead reported was miraculously left undamaged.

When floodwaters damage community spaces, they can interrupt children's programs, create public health concerns through contaminated water and debris, strain local budgets with repeated repairs, and destabilize organizations families rely on for education and safe gathering spaces.

Rebuilding once is expensive, but rebuilding twice can drain time, money, and momentum from nonprofits, workers, and communities already struggling to recover.

Despite repeated damage, Riverside Nature Center has kept its programs going. According to The Kerr County Lead , Sprouts preschool nature classes grew from five families to more than 30 children, and Riverside Rangers and Wildflower Bunch seed-collection walks are still happening.

The center is adding help as it rebuilds. Former Schreiner University intern Bryley Torres joined the staff as the membership and marketing coordinator to support outreach efforts. Looking further ahead, Etzler hopes to expand the visitor center, continue building out the Nature Lab, and one day open an outdoor nature school.

The center is also maintaining its education schedule. A free talk was held on Aug. 19 with Kerr County AgriLife Extension Agent Sam Womble to discuss the New World screwworm and its risks to livestock, ranching, and pets.

articles.title: Another witness ordered released after a fatal shooting by a federal immigration agent in Texas
articles.summary: A second witness to a fatal shooting in Houston by a federal immigration agent has been ordered released from custody after more than a month in detention....
articles.body:
A second witness to a fatal shooting in Houston by a federal immigration agent has been ordered released from custody after more than a month in detention.

Daniel Tirado Pantoja was one of three passengers riding in a work van when the driver, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national who ran a homebuilding business, was shot July 7. The Department of Homeland Security has said Salgado Araujo, who had lived without legal status in the U.S. for 35 years, had "weaponized his vehicle" and that the officer fired on him in self-defense.

U.S. District Judge Alfred Bennett in Houston ordered Tirado Pantoja released after finding that he had no criminal record and was neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community, according to court records.

"We're very glad that Mr. Tirado is going to be reunited with his family," said Ross Miller, an attorney for Tirado Pantoja.

Tirado Pantoja and another passenger, Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego , have disputed accounts given by DHS about the confrontation with agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

They said the agents were never in front of the ICE vehicle and that Salgado Araujo had put vehicle in park as the agents were shooting. Tirado Pantoja also has said the agents' vehicle hit them from behind and then again on the driver's side.

Rojas Pliego was already released from detention last month. DHS did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday about the judge's ruling.

Victor Salgado, the brother of the man killed, was also in the van and remains in custody. He also has asked a judge to order his release.

Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, had said in social media post after the shooting that his father was on his way to work, picking up his workers, when the shooting occurred. He said his father was a hardworking man and was in the process of getting a work permit.

articles.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
articles.summary: They work better than patches, gum or pills, the most up-to-date evidence suggests.
articles.body:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine , which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking.

In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show . Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally.

The review of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws.

It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC.

One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals.

"Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body."

The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.

The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear though, and the NHS says children and non-smokers should never vape.

Doctors say vaping could lead to health harms in children and should be made "less attractive" to them.

Around two in three people who smoke long-term will die from a tobacco-related illness, says the charity Action on Smoking and Health.

According to the World Health Organization, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million people a year.

Quitting smoking reduces your risk of serious illnesses like heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke.

Almost every local NHS stop smoking service provides vapes or other support to help people quit.

You can search online for your local service with your postcode.

articles.title: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – the best pictures so far
articles.summary: The polar bear image taken by Audun Rikardsen was among the 'highly commended' entries in this year's competition.
articles.body:
How would it feel to find yourself face to face with one of the Arctic's most formidable predators?

This stunning image captures life from a seal's perspective. Taken by Norwegian wildlife photographer Audun Rikardsen, it was among the 'Highly Commended' entries in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.

While working as a guide with Arctic Wildlife Tours, Rikardsen rigged an underwater camera with a motion sensor beneath a seal's breathing hole, and then waited. At 4am, a female polar bear approached and peered down.

Rikardsen then waited eight hours for the bear to move away before retrieving the camera and reviewing the images.

When he saw what he had captured, he said: "I was so extremely happy. I was screaming, so I probably woke up all the polar bears for miles."

Rikardsen has previously won two Wildlife Photographer of the Year categories: Birds in 2019 and Oceans: The Bigger Picture in 2025 .

The overall winners will be announced on Tuesday 13 October 2026, followed by an exhibition at the Natural History Museum in London from Friday 16 October 2026.

Scroll down to explore other highly commended works from the competition.

Living alongside polar bears in the Canadian Arctic - BBC World Service

Crockford watched swifts return to London after their annual migration from Africa, filling the air with their high-pitched calls. Most flew too high to photograph, but a few lower-flying ones gave Crockford the opportunity to capture the picture he wanted.

Swifts spend almost their entire lives in the air, usually landing only to nest.

After rainfall, Miyazawa came across an Eastern Japanese toad making its way along a city street. He used a slow shutter speed to photograph it before it hopped back into the bushes.

Eastern Japanese toads are typically found in forests, grasslands and other terrestrial habitats across eastern Japan, but they have also proved remarkably adaptable to urban environments.

Photographer: Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen (Norway)

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Mammals

Location: Kvænangen, Troms County, Norway

Aasen was flying a drone for the Norwegian Orca Survey when he noticed an adult orca carrying the body of a deceased calf through a Norwegian fjord.

The orca repeatedly allowed the calf to sink before bringing it back to the surface, a difficult moment to watch but one that Aasen felt was important to record.

The behaviour may have been an attempt to revive or protect the calf. Killer whales have previously been observed carrying deceased calves, including a case where a female Southern Resident killer whale carried her dead calf for at least 17 days.

A 2026 study suggests that this type of behaviour may be more widespread across the species than previously thought.

Photographer: Andrea & Maceo Grammatico (France)

Category: Highly Commended, Animal Portraits

Location: Sierpe, South Puntarenas, Costa Rica

Only when they reviewed the images did the Grammatico twins realise they had captured a mosquito resting on the head of a fer-de-lance viper. They described it as "one of the most demanding focus stacks we've ever created".

Highly venomous and responsible for more fatal snake bites in Central America than any other species, the fer-de-lance is well camouflaged and can blend into plantation habitats, sometimes going unnoticed by workers.

Location: Meeting of the Waters State Park, Northern Pantanal, Brazil

Parkinson photographed a black vulture perched over a dead yacaré caiman in Brazil's Pantanal wetlands, keeping his boat at a distance and using a long telephoto lens to capture the shot.

A jaguar waiting out of frame emerged after the vulture flew away to claim the carcass. Only then did Parkinson notice a suspiciously clean, straight wound on the back of the caiman's head, possibly caused by a blow from a speeding boat, he suspects.

Photographer: Dewald Tromp (South Africa)

Category: Highly Commended, Animals in their Environment

Location: Namib Desert, near Swakopmund, Namibia

Tromp was photographing a Namaqua chameleon in the Namib Desert when the wind suddenly intensified, bringing a sandstorm that quickly reduced visibility and made breathing difficult.

These chameleons are desert specialists and can obtain moisture directly from the air. Dew gathers on their skin and is channelled towards their mouths through microscopic grooves, while their tongues can also collect fog water condensed on plants, sand and rocks.

Photographer: Bence Máté (Hungary) - 2010 Wildlife Photographer winner

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Birds

Location: Ashnil Aruba Lodge, Tsavo East National Park, Kenya

Máté was watching birds gather at a small pond when tens of thousands of red-billed queleas swept down to drink in the golden late-afternoon light. The movement of so many wings created a rush of air that, he says, could be felt from 30m (98ft) away.

Red-billed queleas can gather in flocks of up to two million and are considered the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with an estimated 1.5 billion breeding adults.

Photographer: Ernest Porter (South Africa)

Location: Manyeleti Game Reserve, Mpumalanga, South Africa

While searching the reserve for wildlife, Porter photographed a red-billed oxpecker rubbing its bill against a white rhino's skin in the afternoon light. The birds feed on insects living on rhinos and can also act as sentinels - calling to warn their hosts when danger approaches. In Swahili, the red-billed oxpecker is known as askari wa kifaru, meaning "the rhino's guard".

Hutton had watched a young leopard pursue a squirrel into a tree, having earlier seen the cat unsuccessfully attempt to stalk a rabbit. The squirrel escaped by climbing higher, leaving the leopard clinging on before it eventually made an awkward retreat.

For young leopards, survival is far from guaranteed: fewer than half reach independence, with male leopards, lions and other predators among the threats they face.

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles

Location: Central Kalahari Game Reserve, Botswana

An African bullfrog lunges for a babul butterfly but misses.

Cullmann had noticed tadpoles on a previous visit after heavy rains and returned the following month to find ponds and puddles full of young bullfrogs. He spent more than two weeks watching the young frogs "eat everything that moved".

As adults, African bullfrogs can reach 12cm (4.7in) in length and spend around 10 months of the year dormant underground, emerging after the rains to breed and feed voraciously.

Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Invertebrates

Location: Wildsumaco Biological Station, Napo Province, Ecuador

Wizen was photographing a lichen dragon katydid measuring just 15mm long, making it difficult to distinguish from the lichen around it. He spotted the insect when it moved, but even then struggled to separate it from its background through the viewfinder.

Found only in Ecuador's Andes Mountains, its spiny armour helps protect it from eagle-eyed predators that can see through its disguise.

Photographer: Shane Gross (Canada) - 2024 Wildlife Photographer winner

Category: Highly Commended, Oceans: The Bigger Picture

Gross was photographing a school of bigeye trevally near the shore at sunrise as a storm approached. To create a split-level image, he turned his camera upside down to aid buoyancy distribution and slowly moved towards the curious fish.

Bigeye trevally are fished in many parts of the world, but here they are relatively safe. In 2023, the waters surrounding D'Arros Island were made a Marine Protected Area and designated as a no-take zone as part of the worldwide initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030.

Category: Highly Commended, Urban Wildlife

Elliott spent hours watching through the kitchen window of a local resident's home, hoping to photograph black bears that frequently pass through the garden. He observed one stopping for a dip in the garden pool, highlighting the increasingly common overlap between wildlife and residential life in Los Angeles County, where housing developments have spread into bear habitat.

Photographer: Ralph Pace (USA) - 2025 Underwater category winner

Category: Highly Commended, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture

A sea hare glides through an eelgrass meadow in the shallows of Monterey Bay, where Pace was photographing in the evening light. He saw the encounter as a hopeful image of "a gentle giant safeguarding the last green meadows of the sea".

By grazing on red algae, that can prevent sunlight reaching the meadow, sea hares play a role in restoring eelgrass, which is vital to coastal ecosystems and an important carbon sink.

Category: Highly Commended, Photojournalism

After learning that a circus featuring animal acts was in town, Rojas went to document it and saw a brown bear riding a small motorcycle, muzzled and secured to the apparatus. For him the scene highlighted the contrast between the animal's wild nature and the human environment imposed upon it.

More than 50 countries around the world have now banned or restricted the use of wild animals in circuses, over concerns it causes them distress .

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London.

articles.title: How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs
articles.summary: A legendary singer-songwriter, her music covered themes around love, loss, female empowerment and spirituality.
articles.body:
The much-loved US singer-songwriter, actress and philanthropist Dolly Parton, who has died aged 80 , was known as the Queen of Country.

Raised in Tennessee, she rose to fame in the late 1960s with hits that bridged country and pop music.

Her songs covered deeply personal themes around growing up poor, love and loss, as well as female empowerment and spirituality.

Live updates: Dolly Parton, legendary US country singer, dies aged 80

Dolly Parton: The country legend who sang from the heart

Following Parton's death, here is a look back at her life through the lens of six iconic songs.

Let's start with Dolly Parton's own personal favourite, her 1971 acoustic country-folk ditty, Coat of Many Colors , external .

The autobiographical track, taken from the album of the same name, tells the heart-stirring tale of how she grew up poor - as one of 12 siblings - but rich in love.

In her book, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics, Parton described it as a "little story" that covers "a world of things", with teachings about bullying, acceptance, love and good parenting.

The lyrics go: " Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my momma made for me " .

The song has been covered by the likes of Shania Twain and Eva Cassidy, and Rolling Stone magazine put it in second place in its list of Parton's top 50 songs , external .

"Had it been the only song she'd ever written, the expression of overwhelming pride and crushing anguish... would have secured her indelible legacy," the US magazine wrote in 2023.

Coat of Many Colors is also the title of Parton's own children's book, and a 2015 TV movie based on her life - starring Alyvia Alyn Lind as the precocious young singer dreaming of fame.

Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, even made her daughter a new patchwork coat to put on display at the museum inside the Dollywood theme park in her home state of Tennessee.

Parton penned many songs about all different aspects of her relationship with her devoted husband Carl Dean , who ran an asphalt paving business in Nashville.

This included the fear that she might lose him, specifically to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage.

We all know her by now, of course, as the infamous Jolene , external .

With its fast fingerstyle minor riff, the song was nominated for a Grammy in 1974 and gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60).

It also showed Parton at her most vulnerable, making it all the more relatable.

Instead of shedding tears or vowing revenge, we hear the protagonist in the song begging the mistress who holds the power to relinquish it.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband," Parton told US media in 2008. "And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us - I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"

Parton had met Dean outside a laundromat on the first day she arrived in Nashville as an 18-year-old aspiring singer. The pair were married for 60 years, until his death in 2025 .

A notoriously private man, he was "a little embarrassed" when she wrote Jolene, Parton said in a 2023 interview with BBC's The One Show , external , adding that "actually, it wasn't as serious [as it sounds]. I was just jealous 'cause she was a beautiful woman and he was just flirting.

"So it gave me a great idea for a song. There's always a Jolene in somebody's life."

She joked that later in life when she saw her, by now, much older husband snoozing in his chair at home, she thought Jolene "can have him now... where's Jolene when you need her?!"

Jolene is her most popular song, having been streamed more than 913 million times on Spotify. Critics from Rolling Stone to the Guardian , external agree it's her best.

BeyoncÃ© gave it a modern rewrite for her 2024 Cowboy Carter , external album, changing the lyrics from: " I'm begging of you, please, don't take my man " to " I'm warning you, don't come for my man. "

Despite the romantic sounding title, this 1974 song , external is actually the sound of Parton tenderly asking her musical mentor, Porter Wagoner, to let her go and pursue her solo career.

Parton was 21 when she joined Wagoner's variety TV show. They released a string of duets and toured together, leading fans to think they were an item.

But they had a complicated relationship, with Parton later writing in another book, Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, that she felt Wagoner saw her rise as a "threat".

"I was making my way as an artist, and he was already an established one. It was his show, but I was trying to grow in the business and grow as an artist myself."

On the track we hear her sing: " Bittersweet memories / That is all I'm taking with me".

Rough Trade's music blog , external once described it as being "heartwarming in its sentiment, crushing in its delivery."

Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song in 1974, but Parton made the difficult decision to back out of the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.

"I said, 'I can't do that'," she told Howard Stern in 2023. "Of course I cried all night about that."

Parton re-recorded I Will Always Love You in 1982 for her starring role in the musical comedy film, The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.

But arguably the most iconic version comes courtesy of Whitney Houston who can be heard booming it out in another film, 1992's The Bodyguard. Her version remains the biggest-selling US single by a female artist.

Parton said she heard the power ballad version for the first time on the radio, and felt so overwhelmed that she had to pull over to avoid crashing her Cadillac.

Whitney Houston took her "little country song" and made it "so much more", she said.

With Parton's newfound professional freedom came a renewed sense of hope, optimism and spirituality - as heard on her 1977 track, Light of a Clean Blue Morning.

She recalled leaving Wagoner's office after their musical split and driving home in a rainstorm, until the clouds parted, giving way to sunlight and an idea for another new song.

Parton - whose earliest performances were in church as a child - referred to it as her "song of deliverance", helping her on the road to stardom.

The lyrics were reworked for the soundtrack to her 1992 romantic comedy film, Straight Talk.

And in early 2026 she released a new charity version of the song , external , in aid of pediatric cancer research, featuring her goddaughter Miley Cyrus, Lainey Wilson, Queen Latifah and Reba.

This defiant anthem of female empowerment, released in 1980, was the most transformative of her career.

Already well established as a singer, 9 To 5 , external brought Parton over into the mainstream popular culture.

She wrote the country-tinged southern soul number as the theme tune for the comedy film of the same name, which saw her make her movie debut alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.

It tells the story of three working women who live out their fantasies of getting even with, and overthrowing, their company's bigot of a boss (played by Dabney Coleman).

The song's distinctive tapping beat at the start is none other than her acrylic nails: "I always play the nails and I'd come up with little things that I would see on the set, like 'I tumble out of bed and I stumble to the kitchen'â¦ And I thought, 'Wow, that sounds like a typewriter,'" she once explained.

Parton won two Grammys for the chart-topping tune, which was also nominated for an Oscar, and later spawned a Broadway musical and a documentary.

A modern day karaoke classic, Parton recorded this hit with fellow US country star Kenny Rogers , external as the lead single for his 1983 album, Eyes That See in the Dark.

The deep love song sold millions of copies and topped both the country and pop charts at the same time.

It was actually written for them by the Bee Gees, intended as a Motown-inspired duet. The Gibb brothers later recorded their own version and performed it live.

Parton and Rogers' rendition, though, remains one of most popular country-pop duets of all time and a classic of the genre.

Their collaboration was "another thing I'm as proud of as anything I ever did in my musical career," she told Smooth Radio , external 40 years on, in 2023.

She added: "You want to do well and keeping up with the likes of Barry [Gibb] and Kenny [Rogers], but I just figure I'll just always be me and do me and that seems to work."

Down from Dover , external - the heartbreaking 1970 tale of an abandoned mother giving birth to a stillborn child was controversial and Wagoner warned Parton against releasing it

The Bargain Store , external - a moving lyrical account of a lady, experienced in love and loss, comparing herself to a secondhand shop, from 1975

Here You Come Again , external - written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil and released by Parton in 1977, it saw her skillfully pivot to pop/soft rock to great effect on her first big crossover hit

articles.title: Jewish, Muslim, Christian Jerusalem Old City vendors say reduced tourism is harming businesses
articles.summary: Vendors pointed to a shortage of flights, high airfares, and lingering fears abroad about security as the main reasons traffic into Israel has suffered. Shop...
articles.body:
Vendors pointed to a shortage of flights, high airfares, and lingering fears abroad about security as the main reasons traffic into Israel has suffered.

Shopkeepers across the Jewish, Muslim, Christian, and Armenian quarters of Jerusalem's Old City say the weakened state of inbound tourism to Israel over the last three years, since the outbreak of war, has put businesses under prolonged strain.

Speaking this week to The Jerusalem Post , vendors pointed to a shortage of flights, high airfares, and lingering fears abroad over security as chief reasons traffic into Israel has been suffering.

"The day-to-day tourism is horrible," Eitan, the owner of Mira, a family-owned shop in the Jewish Quarter, said. "Not too many people. There's not the traffic that there should be."

The main problem, he said, was that there were a reduced number of flights and that the flights that were operating were too expensive for many people, and people are afraid to come."

"I know a lot of people who cancel their — like, sometimes the airline canceled their trip, sometimes they could not come because of the prices," he said. "Once you have limited seats available, not everybody can come."

Eitan, whose family has lived in the Old City since 1968, operated the business since 1984, and has been through "all the intifadas" and "all the wars," said that a meaningful recovery from the tourism slump will remain out of sight until the situation with the airlines improves.

"As long as the airlines are not coming back to Israel, I don't see any solution," he said.

Similar concerns were voiced elsewhere in the Old City.

Dia, a long-time vendor in Jerusalem's Old City Arab Quarter whose family operates the well-known "Alabama – The Heart of Dixie" shop, said the decline in tourism had left business "very, very slow," with many visitors still hesitant to come because of the war.

"It's very safe, the Old City," he said, but due to the image Israel has had abroad since the war began on October 7, 2023, business remained low.

"Three years now, nobody comes," he said.

Hassan, a souvenir vendor near the Church of the Holy Sepulcher in Jerusalem's Christian Quarter, also painted a negative picture, describing business as "very weak" and saying there were "no tourists now."

He recalled that before the war broke out, there was a period of eight to ten months when business was good, "but now, it's zero."

Hassan continued, saying that in his view, the solution lay in bolstering the number of flights coming into Israel.

In the Armenian Quarter, Garo Sandrouni, who operates a ceramics gallery with his wife, Sonia, said that even since the latest major round of strikes between Israel and Iran concluded earlier this year, he had not seen any improvement in the number of tourists coming through.

He said, though, that with the Jewish New Year coming up next month, vendors expected to see some progress.

"Now, everybody is expecting in September that it (the amount of inbound tourism) will be much more. Let's see. But now, there is not much difference from what it was like three months ago or four months ago."

Like other vendors, Garo pointed to the cost of flights as the primary barrier choking off tourism to the country.

"They're much more expensive than before, and some people are also afraid to come," he said.

Sandrouni added that the fear came from three places.

"People are afraid, first from the war, secondly from flights if they cancel, and thirdly from the expensive tickets," he said.

He recalled clients who became stranded in Israel after foreign carriers canceled service, with some eventually traveling to Jordan to fly home.

Sandrouni added that the hits his business has taken over the last three years have been the worst in his four decades of operations.

"I have been here for like 40, 45 years on this street," he said. "It is the worst thing that we have witnessed. I mean, from the October war until today."

Speaking to the Post in June, tourism expert Dr. Eran Ketter pointed to broad structural problems hampering inbound tourism to Israel.

Looking specifically at the US, historically Israel's largest source market, Ketter pointed to geopolitical instability, the stronger shekel, limited air capacity, and higher travel costs as factors suppressing demand.

Tourism expert: Problems around tourism limit visitors to just the highly committed

"Putting all of this together, we're coming into a situation that only people who really want to travel to Israel, and can afford it, are traveling at the moment," he said.

Ketter said greater political stability would be the "number one enabler," allowing the industry to move from a nearly three-year "survival state" into "growth mode."

Stability, he added, would also encourage airlines to resume service, bringing more competition and potentially cheaper fares.

Tourism Ministry Director-General Michael Izhakov , who spoke to the Post the following month, also identified the lack of flight accessibility as a major bottleneck to inbound tourism.

Tourism ministry director-general: With no flights, there is no tourism

"When there are no flights, there is no tourism," he said, adding that the ministry was speaking with airlines and the Transportation Ministry and expected a rapid recovery once flights returned.

"We are waiting only for the flights," he said. "Once the flights reopen, we will see a very rapid recovery in inbound tourism to Israel."

The ministry has also been trying to stimulate demand through marketing and domestic tourism while preparing additional hotel capacity. Izhakov said the ministry had begun targeting Jewish audiences abroad more directly and had shifted some attention toward Israeli tourists when foreign visitors failed to return.

Earlier this month, Izhakov and tourism industry leaders met US Ambassador Mike Huckabee as part of the Israel Tourism Recovery Forum, where, according to the ministry, they discussed expanding direct US-Israel flights.

During the meeting, Huckabee emphasized his personal commitment to promote trips from the US to Israel.

"I will continue encouraging Americans to visit Israel, experience it firsthand, and discover the reality for themselves," the ministry quoted the ambassador as saying.

articles.title: She Posed as a Federal Attorney and Charged a Family Nearly $40,000. Court Records Say They Missed Eight Hearings
articles.summary: An Indiana woman with a prior fraud conviction and two other pending cases is facing a new charge after authorities say she posed as a... Read More
articles.body:
An Indiana woman with a prior fraud conviction and two other pending cases is facing a new charge after authorities say she posed as a federal attorney and collected tens of thousands of dollars from a family seeking help with a Fort Wayne code enforcement dispute.

Katherine Jackson, 42, formerly of Newburgh, allegedly told the family she was licensed to practice law and worked with established law firms in Fort Wayne and Chicago. Police later contacted both firms and were told she had never worked for either one.

Court records say the family paid Jackson more than $34,000 for supposed legal work, consulting services and other expenses while believing she was handling their case.

The arrangement left them with another problem. Eight Neighborhood Code Compliance hearings were held without anyone appearing on their behalf, with each missed hearing carrying a $300 fee, according to 14 News .

She Claimed She Was a Licensed Federal Attorney

The latest case began after a man told police in July that Jackson had offered to represent his family in a dispute with Fort Wayne Neighborhood Code Compliance.

According to 21Alive , the man wanted to pursue what he believed were unwarranted code enforcement fees in federal court. Jackson, an acquaintance, allegedly told him she was a federal attorney, claimed she had passed a law exam and showed him what she represented as her scores.

She also claimed to work for Samuel Bolinger and Associates in Fort Wayne and Prusak and Harkins in Chicago. Investigators later contacted both firms and were told Jackson had never been employed by them. Court records also say she was not licensed as an attorney in Indiana or Illinois.

The Family Paid for Depositions, Audits and Consultants

Investigators say the family made payments for supposed depositions, audits, emails, copies and other legal work. Some payments were made by check or cash, while others were charged through Full Circle Auto, a business associated with Jackson.

She allegedly told the family they also needed a media consulting company and a real estate consultant. Court records say she represented that the media agreement would cost $5,000 and sought money for the other consultant's airfare, hotel and professional fees.

Police later contacted the companies. The media firm said an agreement bearing the family's name appeared to have been altered, while the real estate consultant said he had never heard of Jackson or the family and had never had an Indiana client.

Jackson is charged with one count of fraud in the attorney-impersonation case and was being held at the Allen County Jail when the charge was announced. The attorney-impersonation charge remains pending and has not resulted in a conviction.

They Went to Federal Court and Discovered No Case Had Been Filed

Jackson allegedly appeared with the family at a Neighborhood Code Compliance hearing in February 2024 and then told them they did not need to attend future hearings. Eight later hearings proceeded without the family or anyone acting on their behalf, according to court records.

The situation came to a head after Jackson allegedly told them their federal case was going to trial June 8 at the federal courthouse in Fort Wayne. When the family arrived, they could not find Jackson, a case number or any record of the proceeding they had been expecting. They learned that no federal case had been filed on their behalf, according to 21Alive. Investigators say Jackson stopped communicating with them afterward.

A Separate $8,000 Car Case Is Also Pending

Jackson was charged in another fraud case in July after a man accused her of taking $8,000 to purchase a vehicle that he never received. Earlier reporting says Jackson told the man she owned a car lot and held a dealer's license that would allow her to buy a 2017 Smart Fortwo at a better price.

After receiving the money, she allegedly blamed the delay on repairs and tariffs and asked for additional funds. The man contacted the Virginia dealership advertising the vehicle and learned it had instead been sold to someone in New York.

She Is Awaiting Trial in a Case Involving Her Daughter

Jackson also faces two neglect charges and a fraud charge filed in 2025 following an investigation into representations about her daughter's health.

Investigators said a GoFundMe raised more than $1,500 while describing the child as having Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, suffering dozens of seizures each day and having only months to live. The family also received a Make-A-Wish trip.

A physician who reviewed the child's records concluded there had been extensive maternal falsification and possible medical child abuse, according to court documents. Another doctor said the child does have Pilarowski-Bjornsson syndrome, but described the genetic disorder as chronic rather than terminal.

Jackson's attorneys have disputed the state's allegations and said she did not lie about her daughter's illness to obtain support. That case is scheduled for trial in January.

An Earlier Fundraising Case Resulted in a Conviction

Jackson's older Warrick County case has a different legal status because it ended in a guilty plea. More than a decade ago, while using the name Katherine Conapinski, she was accused of misrepresenting an organization while collecting money connected to a boy with cancer, including funds collected at his funeral.

Jackson accepted a plea agreement and initially received five years of probation, one year of home detention and an order requiring up to $20,000 in restitution. Court records later showed that she violated probation and was sentenced to four years in prison.

Verify a Lawyer's License Before Paying Legal Fees

The Indiana Judicial Branch Roll of Attorneys is the official roster of people licensed to practice law in the state. Consumers can search by name and review an attorney's licensing status rather than relying on business cards, claimed exam scores, contracts or documents provided by the person offering representation.

Clients should also ask for the case number after a lawsuit is filed and independently verify that the case exists. Indiana's MyCase system provides public access to many state court cases, while federal filings can be verified through the appropriate federal court or the federal PACER system.

Unexpected requests for repeated payments for consultants, filing expenses or other services should be accompanied by documentation that can be independently confirmed. If a purported lawyer cannot provide a verifiable license, court case or connection to the law firm they claim to represent, stop sending money until those claims are checked.

articles.title: CIA Director John Ratcliffe on secret trip in Russia
articles.summary: A U.S. Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III transport plane was spotted at a Moscow airport, along with a U.S. diplomatic motorcade, according to public re...
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe is in Moscow, Russia, for meetings, sources familiar with the situation told CBS News on Tuesday.

News of his trip comes after a U.S. Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III transport plane was spotted at a Moscow airport, along with a U.S. diplomatic motorcade. Neither the U.S. nor Russian governments has commented on the identity of the U.S. official in Russia or the purpose of the visit.

It appears to be Ratcliffe's first known trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts.

Ahead of Ratcliffe's trip, the U.S. told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be traveling to Moscow and asked it to suspend strikes until the delegation's departure, according to a senior Ukrainian official.

Ratcliffe's visit comes as recent U.S. intelligence assessments indicate that Putin's risk calculus may be shifting, with the Russian leader potentially increasingly willing to authorize provocative actions against NATO members — including hybrid operations and other deniable measures short of conventional military action — in order to test the resolve of the alliance and the Trump administration.

At this time, U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine remain mostly stalled, with the sides still far apart on core issues.

The CIA has played a role in recent U.S.-Russia detainee exchanges, including the April 2025 release of a U.S.-Russian dual national Ksenia Karelina , whose case Ratcliffe personally negotiated. The agency was also involved in the 2024 prisoner exchange that secured the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich and Marine veteran Paul Whelan.

Former CIA Director William Burns traveled to Moscow in November 2021, when he met with senior Russian officials and spoke directly with President Vladimir Putin to warn him against invading Ukraine.

articles.title: Former Fire Chief Put Department Debit Card on His Personal Cash App, Then Withdrew $6,500, OSBI Says
articles.summary: A former Oklahoma volunteer fire chief is accused of obtaining a debit card connected to his department’s bank account, linking it to his personal Cash... R...
articles.body:
A former Oklahoma volunteer fire chief is accused of obtaining a debit card connected to his department's bank account, linking it to his personal Cash App and using fire department money for himself.

Blake Kendall, 28, formerly served as volunteer fire chief in Mannsville.

The Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation says its probe uncovered more than $1,200 in transactions through his personal Cash App and a separate $6,500 cash withdrawal from Citizens Bank.

Agents also identified other reported cash withdrawals and debit card purchases totaling more than $7,800, according to KXII . Kendall was arrested Aug. 24 in Ardmore and now faces charges of embezzlement and violations of the Oklahoma Computer Crimes Act.

Investigators Say He Linked the Department Card to His Cash App

The investigation began after the Carter County District Attorney's Office asked the OSBI to examine allegations of embezzlement, fraud and computer crime involving the City of Mannsville.

Agents with the agency's Fraud and Cybercrime Unit identified Kendall as a suspect and reviewed financial activity involving the volunteer fire department. According to the OSBI, Kendall obtained a debit card tied to the department's bank account and added it to his personal Cash App. T

Investigators separately identified a $6,500 cash withdrawal from Citizens Bank. The OSBI also reported several other cash withdrawals and debit card purchases totaling more than $7,800.

He Faces Embezzlement and Computer Crime Charges

During the investigation, authorities determined that Kendall is a Chickasaw citizen. The OSBI provided its investigative report to the Chickasaw Lighthorse Police Department and the Chickasaw Nation Office of Tribal Justice Administration. Chickasaw Lighthorse Police arrested Kendall in Ardmore on Aug. 24. He was then booked into the Marshall County Jail.

Kendall was arrested on allegations of embezzlement and violations of the Oklahoma Computer Crimes Act. Kendall has not been convicted. The charges remain accusations and will proceed through the applicable court process.

Public Debit Cards Need Independent Oversight

Organizations entrusted with public money can reduce the opportunity for misuse by separating control of payment cards from responsibility for reviewing the transactions.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office's internal-control standards emphasize preventive controls that safeguard public resources. Those controls include separating incompatible responsibilities so one person does not control authorization, spending and review.

Unexplained cash withdrawals, transfers to personal payment apps and transactions without supporting documentation should receive prompt review. Access should also be removed when an official or employee no longer needs a card, and organizations can use transaction alerts and limits to flag unusual activity before losses accumulate.

When suspected misuse is discovered, financial statements, card records, Cash App or other payment-service records, receipts and authorization documents should be preserved for auditors and investigators.

articles.title: Elissa Slotkin calls out Hasan Piker for blaming Jewish Americans targeted over their Israel views
articles.summary: Hasan Piker warned that American Jews could face violence over Israel support, prompting senators Elissa Slotkin and Jacky Rosen to condemn his remarks.
articles.body: Democratic Sens. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev., condemned livestreamer Hasan Piker after he said that Jewish Americans will face inevitable consequences for supporting Israel. Last week, Piker told his viewers, "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews." Slotkin, who is widely believed to be a potential contender for the 2028 presidential election, shared what she called a "response to Hasan Piker's recent comments on Jews in America being targeted because of their views on Israel." And blaming the victims of violence for bringing it on themselves only further endangers people." ANTISEMITIC STREAMER FINALLY MAKES DEM LEADER SNAP WITH RARE REBUKE: ‘MALICIOUS’ She suggested that this is part of a much larger phenomenon of the normalization of political violence. "In a time where political violence and anti-semitism has been spiking — and where just 6 months ago Michigan had a nearly deadly event of anti-semitic mass violence at Temple Israel — no one should causally be suggesting that anyone, Jews or otherwise, are to blame for being targeted," Slotkin concluded. Rosen offered a similar statement, blasting Piker’s remarks as "a new low." "Hasan Piker has been trafficking in antisemitic tropes for a while but even this is a new low," she posted to X. Let me be absolutely clear: crimes against Jews for being Jews is antisemitism plain and simple. There’s no excuse for it." ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Many prominent politicians across the aisle, including fellow Democrats, have spoken out directly against Piker, arguing that he appears to be victim-blaming the Jewish community for attacks they endure.
